item.title: Things to Do in NYC This Week (Nov 9 - Nov 15)
item.description: Art Week, a chili cook-off, and a 10-seat supper club
item.dc:creator: Alexa Weiser
item.content:encoded:
I spent the weekend in Hudson celebrating a friend’s birthday. At least most of the weekend. After watching a scary movie Saturday night, we said goodnight and went off to our rooms. About 10 minutes later someone sent a text that it “kinda smells like rotten eggs.” That’s all it took to send us into a full group panic, convinced there was a gas leak. We packed up and got into our cars within minutes and started the drive back to the city. It turns out it was just the smell of the well water. I’m sure the scary movie while we were in a cabin had nothing to do with it.

Before that, the weekend was perfect. We hiked, sampled pastries, played games, and drank cider. We also squeezed in a dinner in town at feast & floret, a rustic, flower-filled restaurant that we ended up closing for the night, enjoying a pomegranate panna cotta they stuck a candle in so we could sing to our friend. Waking up in the city on Sunday after driving into the night was both jarring and kind of a relief to avoid traffic. I think the dogs were the real ones to lose out.

Monday November 9

New York: A Documentary Film, Shadows of the Past Screening and Q&A
SVA Theatre | 6-9pm at 333 W 23rd St, Chelsea

Open House New York, the nonprofit behind the annual OHNY Weekend, hosts the first full public viewing of Episode 9 of Ric Burns' documentary series New York: A Documentary Film, in its 25th anniversary year. The episode covers the second half of the 20th century, from the city's near-bankruptcy in 1975 through the crime of the 80s and 90s, 9/11, financial meltdowns, superstorms, and Covid, and the comeback that followed. The screening is followed by a Q&A with Burns and co-writer and co-producer James Sanders, moderated by Cassim Shepard. Episode 10 screens the following Monday, November 16. Tickets are $12.

Subscribe for the best things to do in NYC.

Inside the Pergamon: Ancient Wonders, Berlin Stories
Black Forest Brooklyn | 6:30-10:30pm at 181 Smith St, Cobble Hill

Dr. Pinar Durgun, an archaeologist and art historian who used to curate at Berlin's Pergamon Museum and now heads the ancient Western Asian seals department at the Morgan Library, talks about the ancient wonders inside the Pergamon and the stories behind them. The museum sits on Berlin's Museum Island, and closed its doors in 2023 for more than a decade. Durgun will discuss what happens when one of the world’s most extraordinary museums closes its doors with some of its biggest treasures still inside. From Babylon’s spectacular blue Ishtar Gate to the Market Gate of Miletus, the Pergamon Altar, and objects spanning thousands of years of ancient Western Asian history, the museum is a monument itself. Tickets are $29.

Tuesday November 10

⭐ Opening reception of Julie Curtiss: UNREAL
Gagosian | 6-8pm at 541 W 24th St, Chelsea

Julie Curtiss's first presentation with Gagosian in New York, and her first New York solo show in five years. There’s a bunch of opening receptions almost daily, but I’m featuring this one because Julie makes the city her painting’s subject. Faceless figures in apartments, laundromats, and bodegas, rendered in her surreal, polished style. On view through December 19. No RSVP needed.

The 2026 Brooklyn Martini Lunch
Elsa | 5:30-7:30pm at 136 Atlantic Ave, Brooklyn Heights

A fundraiser for Electric Literature, the literary nonprofit and publisher behind Electric Lit. They’re dedicated to making literature more exciting, relevant, and inclusive for all. Despite the name, it’s an evening happy hour at Elsa, with a complimentary gin or vodka martini included. Tickets are $60.

S.T.A.R.E.: A Digital Wellness Audit w/ Dan Fox
Bar Heretic | 8-10pm at 270 Clermont Ave, Fort Greene

S.T.A.R.E. is a communal digital wellness check-up hosted by Dan Fox, a Fort Greene resident and slow-tech advocate who works with Light Phone and runs phone-free gatherings. Come with a vague sense that your smartphone is ruining your life and leave with a plan to improve your relationship to it, over wine and snacks at Bar Heretic. Tickets are $25.

Diwali Celebration at the Seaport Museum
South Street Seaport Museum | 4-6pm at 213 Water St, Seaport

The South Street Seaport Museum is celebrating Diwali with the Culture Tree Collective and the Rubin Museum. There will be henna from 4 to 5pm, Diwali Puppet Storytime at 4:15pm in the Maritime City gallery, an interactive dance workshop at 5pm, and hands-on art activities on the Water Street cobblestones, including decorating a diya lamp to float in a pool. RSVP for free.

Wednesday November 11

⭐ Art Week NYC
Various galleries citywide | November 11-14 in Manhattan

The first Art Week NYC, a four-day citywide program organized by Artforum, ARTnews, and Art in America, with more than 80 galleries and 30 cultural institutions taking part. Days are organized by neighborhood, Chelsea, Tribeca, SoHo, the Lower East Side, and the Upper East Side, with coordinated evening openings, artist walkthroughs, talks, performances, and walking tours, plus a Midtown hub. The anchor public program is the New Museum's day of talks on Saturday. Check out the full schedule.

Fado Night at Leitao
Leitao | 8-11pm at 547 Hudson St, West Village

Leitao, the West Village Portuguese restaurant, hosts its monthly fado night. Chef Nuno Sousa cooks a four-course dinner, paired with four Portuguese wines and a welcome cocktail, with live fado performed between courses in the cellar, where the crowd stays silent for the music. Seating is communal, and the menu leans on lamb, pork, and seafood. Tickets start at $165.

⭐ The Bowery Review: Issue Launch Party
KGB Bar | 7pm at 85 E 4th St, East Village

The Bowery Review, the quarterly print humor magazine edited by Tim Latterner, launches its fifth issue at KGB Bar. Latterner, a former writer for National Lampoon, MAD, and Playboy’s humor section, started the magazine because the outlets he came up in are gone or don’t publish new humor anymore, and he wanted to make the one he wanted to read. Each issue is funny short stories, one-liners, cartoons, and essays from writers and cartoonists who’ve written for The New Yorker, McSweeney’s, and MAD. Pick up a copy of the new issue, have a drink, and hear readings from the city’s funniest writers. RSVP for free.

Thursday November 12

⭐ 25th Anniversary Exhibition: Masterworks from the Neue Galerie
Neue Galerie | Opens November 12 at 1048 Fifth Ave, Upper East Side

The Neue Galerie reopens all of its galleries after a three-month restoration of its Fifth Avenue mansion, with a 25th-anniversary exhibition drawn mostly from its own collection of early 20th-century Austrian and German art and design. Klimt's Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I anchors the show, alongside Schiele, Kandinsky, Munter, and recent acquisitions. The museum, founded in 2001, recently announced it will merge with the Met in 2028. While it’s exciting in ways, I want to enjoy the Neue as is as much as possible beforehand and this is a great way to do so. On view through January 11. Tickets are $28.

Operation MAHA: Mission Accomplished?
Sugar Mouse NYC | 6:30-8:30pm at 47 3rd Ave, East Village

Unmuted, the debate series where talking points go to die, hosts a live debate on whether RFK Jr. has made American medicine better or worse. Biomedical engineer and women's health advocate Kerry Semle argues it out with Emily Kaplan, CEO of the Broken Science Initiative, over vaccines, women's health, and scientific research. If you feel like getting angry, this is the place to be. Tickets are $10.

⭐ The City Speaks
Henry Street Settlement | 6:30-8pm at 265 Henry St, Lower East Side

The New York Adventure Club presents a one-man show on New York slang, accents, and speech, led by performer and creator Nic Reale, who plays a cast of Lower East Side characters. Part linguistic deep dive and part interactive performance, it traces how generations of immigration shaped the way New Yorkers talk. Fittingly, it takes place inside the Henry Street Settlement, the Lower East Side institution founded in 1893. Tickets are $45.

Gowanus Wharf Block Party
Gowanus Wharf | 4-7pm at 340 Nevins St, Gowanus

Gowanus Wharf celebrates the opening of its new public waterfront park at Nevins Landing with a neighborhood block party along the Gowanus Canal. There will be local pop-ups, live music, games, and public art, including work by Jen Lewin and Tom Fruin. A first look at the new park on its opening day. RSVP for free.

Friday November 13

NY Comedy Festival Presents Ilana Glazer Live!
Beacon Theatre | 6:45pm at 2124 Broadway, Upper West Side

Ilana Glazer, the Broad City co-creator and stand-up, brings her live show to the Beacon as part of the 22nd annual New York Comedy Festival. Glazer is really having a moment. Her second special, Human Magic, is on Hulu, and she made her Broadway debut this year in Good Night, and Good Luck. Tickets start at $62.

⭐ Studio Tropical Supper Club
Studio Tropical | 7-10pm at 20 Grand Ave, Clinton Hill

Colombian chef and artist Stephanie Bonnin opens Studio Tropical, her Clinton Hill culinary studio and the home of her LaTropiKitchen supper clubs, as an intimate 10-guest communal-table supper club. She’ll serve seven courses of Caribbean and Latin American food rooted in the Colombian Caribbean, with vinyl from Bonnin's personal collection and Colombian art on the walls. Sounds like a perfect evening. Tickets are $140 with an optional $70 wine pairing. Every Friday & Saturday moving forward.

Fall 2026 Jazz Jam
Brooklyn Conservatory of Music | 6-10:30pm at 58 Seventh Ave, Park Slope

The Brooklyn Conservatory of Music, the Park Slope community music school, is hosting an open jazz jam with its jazz faculty and students. Student and adult musicians can sit in on guided sessions and listeners can drop in for an informal evening of live music. The 6 to 8pm session is for kids and the 8:30 to 10:30pm session is for adults. RSVP for free.

Saturday November 14

A Current Affair: Pop Up Vintage Market
Industry City | 12-5pm at 51 34th St, Sunset Park

A Current Affair, the vintage pop up fair, returns to Brooklyn for two days in the Box Factory at Industry City. More than 70 premier vintage retailers and private dealers from both coasts sell clothing, accessories, and jewelry from the Victorian era to today. You know it’s a good one when it made it into my Vintage Shopping guide. Tickets are $22.

⭐ Site Conditions: Five Talks on Art and the City
New Museum | 11am-6pm at 235 Bowery, Lower East Side

The New Museum and Artforum co-present a full day of talks for Art Week NYC. Five sessions on how art gets made and shown in the city now. The lineup runs from Technologies of Power at 11am, with Ian Cheng, Aria Dean, Simon Denny, Jill Magid, and Julia Weist, through Working Conditions at 12:30pm, Paul Chan on his AI self-portrait at 2pm, Artists at the Movies at 3:30pm, and Architecture for Art at 5pm, with Elizabeth Diller, Annabelle Selldorf, and Shohei Shigematsu on designing new buildings for the Frick, MoMA, and the New Museum. I’m surprisingly most drawn to the architecture talk. Tickets are $15.

NY Cider Festival NYC
Red Hook Barrel Yard | 11am-4pm at 185 Van Dyke St, Red Hook

The New York Cider Association brings more than 25 cider producers from across New York State to Red Hook Cidery for a day of tasting, with live music and food, plus cider and food pairing sessions. Pourers include Angry Orchard, Brooklyn Cider House, Nine Pin Ciderworks, and Original Sin Cider. A very fall way to spend a Saturday. Tickets are $40.

The 1st Chomps Chili Cookoff
Essex Kitchen | 2-5pm at 88 Essex St, Lower East Side

Chomps, the meat snack brand, hosts its first annual chili cook-off at Essex Kitchen. They’re doing it as a fundraiser for the Food Education Fund, the nonprofit that teaches culinary skills to high school students across the city. If you think you make the best chili in New York City, this one’s for you. Register for free.

Sunday November 15

⭐ Play Fair Brooklyn
Bogart House | 1-5pm at 230 Bogart St, Bushwick

Play Fair, a community festival from Find Play, turns Bogart House into a club fair for North Brooklyn. Built around the idea that cities make it hard to meet people, they aim to help locals find a sense of belonging in their community. More than 20 local clubs, volunteer groups, and businesses host 20+ activities and workshops. Pottery, beading, arts and crafts, knitting, chess, yoga, pilates, board games, journaling, breathwork, rock climbing, and even dog adoption. Tickets are $30.

Make Your Own Advent Calendar at The Standard
La Maison du Chocolat | 12-3:30pm at 848 Washington St, Meatpacking District

La Maison du Chocolat sets up at The Standard's ice rink plaza for you to build your own advent calendar from 26 of their chocolates, handcrafted in Paris. I got to go to a preview and I felt like a little kid picking my chocolates and noting which day had which variety. Tickets are $125 and cover a pair, including the calendar box, 26 chocolates of your choosing, plus a macaron and hot cocoa.

Source Notes Guided Tasting with Kettl Founder Zach Mangan
Kettl Matcha Sen Mon Ten | Multiple seatings at 38 Norman Ave, Greenpoint

Source Notes is Kettl founder Zach Mangan's new series where he tastes through the Kettl catalog and shares the stories behind each tea, the people, places, and seasons that make it unique. This in-person session tastes three special matchas with their sourcing stories, plus a traditional wagashi sweet pairing and a Q&A on all things matcha. It’s intimate with only eight seats per session. Tickets are $90.

What I did last week.

Places or shows I went to over the last week. These are personal recommendations. If I had a cool week, they’ll be cool. If I didn’t, they won’t.

  1. Salon + Art - Hosted in the Park Avenue Armory for its 15th year, Salon + Art presents the best vintage, modern, and contemporary design, curating a show from 30+ exhibitors. It was magical to walk through. It ended on Sunday but will be back next year. Plus there’s plenty more coming up at the Armory.

  2. Passerine - Finally tried the Indian bistro by Chef Gaurav Bhatla. While it’s rooted in Indian flavor, I would almost call it New York fusion. The menu includes a lobster roll, a burrata, and a beef pot pie, all with Indian spices.

  3. Auserman Chocolate - A Substack friend (see, they’re real!) invited me to join her at a chocolate tasting at the Yale Club. I mostly said yes to catch up with her and peek behind the curtain at the private club, but I left already ordering chocolate from the Ecuadorian brand we sampled all night. Auserman not only uses beans from Ecuador, but actually makes the chocolate there too. A great pick if you’re looking for holiday gift add-ons.

  4. Li Hei Di & Lucas Samaras at Pace Gallery - I previewed the new exhibitions at Pace and wow. Both were incredible. I rarely come across paintings that suck you in so much that you just have to stare the way Li’s do. And Samaras’ Boxes and Reconstructions exhibit is literally box sculptures pulled together with the most every day materials that he somehow makes feel magical. Worth a visit before they close in January.

  5. Tristan & Yseult - After years of world touring, the show returns to St Ann’s Warehouse. It tells a love story that has deep humor built in, alongside low-fi aerial acrobatics and live band. It’s a bit of everything and is unlike anything you’ve seen. I promise. Only a few weeks left to catch the show.

item.title: Things to Do in NYC This Week (Nov 2 - Nov 8)
item.description: Mice, diners, and gingerbread
item.dc:creator: Alexa Weiser
item.content:encoded:
I woke up early to write this letter and heard the unmistakable sound of mice in the walls (hopefully the walls) from our small office room. This wouldn’t be our first encounter with mice in the apartment, despite having a prey dog who’s supposed to be aware of this stuff, but it might be the final nudge I need to move. I’ve been in Prospect Heights for almost 5 years. It might be my favorite neighborhood, but I’m also ready for a change.

One of the things that’s so special about living in NYC for me is getting to build your little neighborhood community. Finding your coffee shop, your deli, your daily walk, even your dry cleaner. I’m ready to experience that in a different neighborhood. I’m fairly set on staying in South Brooklyn, but the Upper West Side has also been on my radar. Pitch me your neighborhood to help me out.

In other news, holiday events and pop-ups are in full swing. The arrival of the tree at Rockefeller this week kind of signals the beginning for me. I’m going to celebrate by seeing jazz in a dark lounge instead of braving the crowds.

Monday November 2

⭐ SPARK Musical Theatre Festival
SPARK | November 2-22 at 15 W 28th St, Chelsea

The SPARK Musical Theatre Festival is the inaugural festival of new musicals from Emerging Artists Theatre, with 26 short and full-length works in development. Performances run November 2-22 at the 28th Street Theatre, each followed by a post-show talkback, with highlights including The Selkie Bride on November 22 and a staged reading of The Great Mortality on November 12 and 13. Tickets range, check out their full line up. It’s a great way to see something new without breaking the bank.

Subscribe for the best things to do in NYC.

How to Listen
Lifeshop | 8-10pm at 199 N 8th St, Williamsburg

How to Listen is an interactive evening in a candlelit Williamsburg loft on the practice of real listening. The session covers what gets in the way of listening, what to do instead, and how to ask questions that make people feel safe, seen, and heard. Tickets are $40 and readers get 20% off with code HAPPENINGS. While I haven’t been to this specific workshop, I’ve thoroughly enjoyed every other Lifeshop event. They’re interactive and always leave me deeply reflecting on my life.

Day of the Dead Family Celebration
Green-Wood Cemetery | 4-7pm at 500 25th St, Greenwood Heights

The Day of the Dead Family Celebration is a free afternoon at Green-Wood marking Día de los Muertos with crafts, performances, music, and food. Hands-on activities run 4-5:30pm, including a papier-mâché alebrije scavenger hunt, charm making, and marigold seed planting, followed by mariachi, Banda de los Muertos, and dance performances start at around 5:15pm. The Historic Chapel ofrenda is open 4-6:15pm, with a closing ceremony at 6:30pm. Register for free.

Tuesday November 3

Backgammon Night
The Maze | 7:30-9:30pm at 43 W 24th St, Flatiron

Backgammon Night is the Village Backgammon Club's casual game night at The Maze, the Flatiron alcohol-free members club with a food program from Tom Colicchio's Crafted Hospitality. Play is casual and all levels are welcome. Tickets are $20 and include a mocktail.

⭐ Counter Culture: NYC's Greatest Diners and Luncheonettes
Spanish Benevolent Society | 6pm at 239 W 14th St, Chelsea

Counter Culture is a talk by photographers James and Karla Murray on their book about New York City's greatest diners and luncheonettes. The book profiles 30 Manhattan spots, from Lexington Candy Shop, Veselka, Tom's Restaurant, and B&H Dairy to newer places like Thai Diner and Golden Diner, with profiles by food journalist Emma Orlow. Register for free. Nothing feels more New York.

Wednesday November 4

Freaks of Nature: Paint & Sip
Pour Toi x Apartment 5 | 6:30-9pm at 157 Ludlow St, Lower East Side

Pour Toi's monthly blind-box paint and sip gives everyone an art kit and a prompt with a theme. This one is Freaks of Nature, taking cues from bioluminescence, bizarre botanicals, and otherworldly organisms. Tickets are $38 or $48 if you want it accompanied with a pour of wine.

NYC Salt: The Next Generation of Visual Storytellers
The National Arts Club | 7pm at 15 Gramercy Park South, Gramercy Park

NYC Salt: The Next Generation of Visual Storytellers is a presentation with NYC Salt founder Alicia Hansen at the National Arts Club. The nonprofit engages, inspires, and empowers New York City youth through photography instruction, mentorship, and college-preparatory guidance. At this talk, Hansen discusses the organization's mission and impact, and how the camera serves as a catalyst for self-discovery and career opportunity, while students and alumni present their own work, showing how they document their families, communities, and cultures. RSVP for free.

Thursday November 5

⭐ For the Love of Food Magazines
Museum of Arts and Design | 6-8pm at 2 Columbus Circle, Columbus Circle

A Society of Publication Designers panel on food magazines, with Caroline Newton (creative director, Bon Appétit), Aliza Abarbanel (co-founder and co-editor, Cake Zine), Thomas Payne (visuals director, Saveur), Ann Martin Foley (art director, Food & Wine), and Alex Tatusian (worker-owner, Buffet), moderated by Dan Pelosi. They talk early memories of food and art, how the industry has changed, and where food media goes next. They should probably add some food Substackers to the line up. Tickets are $20 and online sales close Wednesday.

Sketching & Bookbinding Workshop
Liz's Book Bar | 6-8pm at 315 Smith St, Carroll Gardens

A three-part, hands-on workshop combining sketching, portrait drawing, and bookbinding, taught by Brooklyn artist Sharon Y. Li. Draw self-portraits from traditional techniques and odd prompts, then bind the sketches into a simple notebook to keep filling. No experience needed and all supplies are provided. Tickets are $53.

⭐ Curt Bloch and His Underwater Cabaret
Museum of Illustration | 6:30-8:30pm at 128 E 63rd St, Upper East Side

A Society of Illustrators evening on Curt Bloch, the German-Jewish writer, poet, and artist who made booklets while in hiding from the Nazis in the Netherlands from 1943 to 1945. The program shows digital archival images of the recently discovered booklets, with a lecture and poetry reading from Thilo von Debschitz, Simone Bloch (Curt Bloch's daughter), and poet Samuel Haecker, who reads Bloch's poems. Presented in partnership with the German Consulate General New York. Tickets are $15.

Lamb Jam Finale
Platform by the James Beard Foundation | 6:30pm at 25 11th Ave, Chelsea

The Lamb Jam Finale is the closing dinner of Lamb Jam, the American Lamb Board's annual chef competition celebrating American lamb, held at Platform by the James Beard Foundation. The 2026 champions, Cody Chassar of Gunshow in Atlanta and Francis Ang of Abacá in San Francisco, cook alongside Lamb Jam all-stars Will Gilson of Amba Cambridge in Boston and Kareem El Ghayesh of KG BBQ in Austin. Guests taste each chef's signature Lamb Jam dish, then two new East Coast-West Coast collaborations created for the finale, with a cocktail reception, wine pairings, and a Q&A with the chefs. The evening ends with a vote on the best lamb dish. Tickets start at $185.

Friday November 6

⭐ The Sturbridge Show NYC
The Altman Building | Friday & Saturday at 135 W 18th St, Chelsea

The New York edition of the 40-year Sturbridge antiques fair, centered on vintage sourcing and design research. Over 90 dealers from the US and UK show antique and vintage fashion, textiles, jewelry, accessories, and rare pieces, and this edition adds a dedicated menswear floor for the first time, with vintage menswear, denim, workwear, tailoring, and archival pieces. I’ve been on the hunt for high quality men’s vintage so I can continue playing dress up with my husband. Tickets start at $25.

⭐ New York Comedy Festival
NY Comedy Festival | Through November 15 at various venues

The 22nd annual New York Comedy Festival opens Friday, with more than 100 shows across all five boroughs through November 15. Opening night includes the Tokyo Kanpai Boys at New York Comedy Club East Village, Ziwe at Town Hall, Gayme Show with Matt Rogers and Dave Mizzoni at BMCC Tribeca Performing Arts Center, Adam Ray at Gramercy Theatre, and Dave Chappelle at Madison Square Garden. Tickets vary by show. Check out the full line up.

Part Two: Luxury Marketplace
Seven Moods | Friday-Sunday from 1pm-5pm at 282 11th Ave, Chelsea

Part Two is a luxury vintage marketplace bringing together 40+ established vintage businesses, with rare vintage bags, vintage designer suits, and a bridal salon of dresses from the 40s to 60s. This is its return after the SoHo debut. Despite my vintage addiction, I haven’t actually checked out this show yet so give me your takes if you end up going. Tickets are $21.

⭐ Salon Art + Design
Park Avenue Armory | Friday-Sunday at 643 Park Ave, Upper East Side

Salon Art + Design is a fair for collectible design and fine art, back at the Park Avenue Armory for its 15th edition. Around 40 international galleries plus 10 special design exhibitions show museum quality furniture, lighting, ceramics, glass, jewelry, sculpture, textiles, painting, and decorative arts, with a Vitra presentation marking Verner Panton's 100th birthday among the highlights. I’m going to the press preview on Wednesday so keep an eye on the City Happenings chat for a review before the weekend. Single day tickets start at $37.

⭐ Gingerbread NYC: The Great Borough Bake-Off
Museum of the City of New York | Opens November 6 at 1220 Fifth Ave, East Harlem

Gingerbread NYC: The Great Borough Bake-Off is the Museum of the City of New York's annual exhibition of city icons recreated in gingerbread, returning for its fifth year. Bakers from across the five boroughs build on the theme "Iconic New York," turning distinctive buildings, places, and symbols into candy-lined streets and edible skyscrapers. A panel of judges awards multiple themed prizes, and visitors vote during the run for the People's Choice award. This year's judges are Magnolia Bakery's Bobbie Lloyd, the Met's Nadine Orenstein, Amy's Bread founder Amy Scherber, and Melba's owner Melba Wilson. Tickets are $23.

Cultures of Perfume
Rizzoli Books | 6-7:45pm at 1133 Broadway, Flatiron

Cultures of Perfume is a smell-enlivened discussion between author Saskia Wilson-Brown and writer Rachel Syme at Rizzoli, timed to Wilson-Brown's new book The Cultures of Perfume: Scents That Shaped History. Wilson-Brown founded the Los Angeles-based Institute for Art and Olfaction in 2012, a nonprofit advancing access and experimentation in perfumery, and the book is an illustrated field guide to 36 scent notes. Described as a people's history of perfume, it tells the story of smell and humanity's fascination with perfume through anecdotes, historical research, and folk knowledge, with a "Smell More" section after each chapter pointing readers to scents by independent brands. RSVP for free.

Saturday November 7

Material Matters
Iron23 | Saturday and Sunday at 29 W 23rd St, Flatiron

Ok it really is a weekend to shop. A home show from the team behind Manhattan Vintage and Artists & Fleas so you know it’s going to be good. More than 55 exhibitors rooted in home will be on display: furniture, objects, décor, and art spanning contemporary to vintage. Tickets start at $22.

⭐ NYC Autumn Wine and Food Festival
Crush Wine | 1-8pm at 440 Grand St, Lower East Side

The NYC Autumn Wine and Food Festival is the 12th annual fall wine festival from Crush Wine Experiences, a company of wine professionals and sommeliers, in the Grand Hall's rustic tasting room. More than 100 sommelier-curated wines and craft beverages pour from France, Italy, Spain, Slovenia, Greece, Georgia, South America, South Africa, California, and New York State, alongside bites from artisan food makers. Tickets start at $61.

Exploring the Seaside Village of City Island
City Island Nautical Museum | 1-3pm at 190 Fordham St, City Island

Exploring the Seaside Village of City Island is a guided walk of the Bronx seaside community led by a City Island resident. The walk covers the island's history from mulberry orchards to oystering and boat building, with a visit to a historic private waterfront property featured in The Royal Tenenbaums, a stroll downtown, and a peek inside the Nautical Museum. Tickets are $40.

Mindful Matter Market No.05: The November Market
Mindful Matter Market | November 7-8, 1-7pm at 327 W 36th St, Garment District

Mindful Matter Market is a two-day plant-based food and sustainable fashion market, back in New York for its fifth edition. The November Market gathers 25+ plant-based and natural brands across vegan food and drinks, herbal apothecary, natural beauty, and sustainable goods, plus live music, tastings, talks, and practitioner treatments and consultations throughout the weekend. Tickets are $15.

Sunday November 8

Gary's Backyard Mushroom Walk
Central Park | 10am-3pm at W 102nd St and Central Park West, Upper West Side

Gary's Backyard Mushroom Walk is a guided mushroom walk in Central Park with the New York Mycological Society, honoring Gary Lincoff, who traversed Central Park countless times, often with the club in tow. The society's walks observe, identify, and document the city's mushrooms, and this one is a look-don't-pick walk, not a foraging walk. Bring water and lunch, and protect against mosquitoes and ticks. Join NYMS to register. Still shocked that the last mushroom walk I featured was my most engaged with event. Couldn’t pass up adding this one.

⭐ New York Sign Museum Tour
New York Sign Museum | 1-2pm at 2465 Atlantic Ave, East New York

A guided tour of the New York Sign Museum, a registered nonprofit preserving historic signage from around the New York metropolitan area, housed inside the Noble Signs workshop. The collection includes over 40 full-scale rescued storefront signs plus dozens of smaller pieces and ephemera, shown in a prewar factory space with glass block walls, art deco tin ceilings, stained glass dividers, and a functioning dumbwaiter, where signs are still made the old-fashioned way. The museum started in 2019, when Noble Signs founder David Barnett and cofounder Mac Pohanka began saving signs that would otherwise be lost when their businesses closed. Tickets are $30.

RAW Wine New York
Raw Wine | November 8-9 at 33 35th St, Sunset Park

RAW Wine New York is North America's largest fair devoted to organic, biodynamic, and low-intervention wine, marking its tenth anniversary in New York, with wines from more than 100 producers. The fair is a chance to meet the people behind the bottles, from growers to importers, and runs Sunday and Monday. A separate anniversary after-party follows Sunday at 6pm at Have and Meyer in Williamsburg, with natural sparkling wine, a signature cocktail, cheese and charcuterie, pasta, desserts, and live swing jazz. Tickets start at $30.

What I did last week.

Places or shows I went to over the last week. These are personal recommendations. If I had a cool week, they’ll be cool. If I didn’t, they won’t.

  1. Drew Michael: Love Me - Wow do I love small theatre. Comedian Drew Michael takes you on a deeply felt, immersive journey through his mind. I can’t say much more without giving it away, but it was incredibly well done for a 1-person show. I laughed hard and even teared up. Go see it before it closes on November 22nd.

  2. Dante Aperitivo - My friend turned 32 on Monday and we decided to grab a last minute celebratory bite. We ended up sharing a burger 3 ways (which I wouldn’t recommend here given how messy it was to cut) alongside fries and a pasta with this thick bolognese. It was delicious and easy.

  3. Schoelkopf Gallery 25|250 - Schoelkopf turned 25 and given it lines up with America’s 250th anniversary, they’re putting on a joint celebration with a landmark program of exhibitions, scholarship, and events that recognize the legacy and evolution of American art. I went to the preview last week and would definitely check it out before the show closes on January 16th.

  4. Roscioli - I guess it’s my lucky week because I also walked into Roscioli for an early dinner and got seated immediately at the counter. Nothing new for me, but I will never pass up their pan tomate.

  5. I Became We - A first-person monologue performed by a sixteen-person choir about a woman in her mid-thirties wrestling with one of life’s most important decisions. I was intrigued by the premise but didn’t expect it to be laugh out loud funny. It was. And I’ve never seen anything like it. Running through November 22nd if you want to check it out.

item.title: Things to Do in NYC This Week (Oct 26 - Nov 1)
item.description: Tuna cutting, bracelet making, and 60,000 runners
item.dc:creator: Alexa Weiser
item.content:encoded:
For my husband’s birthday I pretended we were 25 again and planned a full Saturday marathon: a 5k out in Flushing Meadows, lawn games with our friends, and two full concerts back to back.

There was a time when a Saturday like this needed no occasion. I planned this one for weeks, and I loved every part of it, right up until a crew wanted to go do karaoke after the last set and I realized I had met my end. Thank god for venues with noise ordinances by 10pm. I was in bed by 11.

Monday October 26

Jeff Yang: Pop Culture and James Hong
Think!Chinatown | 6:30-8:30pm at 1 Pike St, Chinatown

Author Jeff Yang is discussing Asian American pop culture and his new book about actor James Hong. You might not know actor James Hong’s name, but he has over 700 acting credits from Mulan to Everything Everywhere All at Once. The autobiography draws on never-before-seen archival materials and hours of interviews. Free, no RSVP needed.

Subscribe for the best things to do in NYC.

The Reckoning: Selected Scenes and Conversation
Teatro LATEA | 7-9pm at 107 Suffolk St, Lower East Side

Verbatim theater from Ukraine’s war, live on stage. One man stayed in his village outside Kyiv when everyone else fled, and this is his story, drawn from verified survivor testimony of Russia’s war in Ukraine. Co-writer and director Josephine Burton brings newly adapted excerpts performed by US-based Ukrainian actors, ahead of the production’s full North American tour in 2027, and leads a conversation afterward with Sevhil Musaieva Borovyk on the testimony behind the work. Part of Razom for Ukraine’s Ukrainian Cultural Festival. Tickets are by donation.

⭐ Four Top: A One Act Comedy by Kyle Beechey
Casino | 7pm at 171 East Broadway, Lower East Side

The Restaurant Diaries is a series of one-act comedies staged like you’re a fly on the wall for an evening. Tonight is Four Top, a show where two couples find themselves on a blind date with wildly different expectations. Casino provides the space and cocktails. They’re trying to make theatre feel less serious by bringing it to a casual environment where you can have a snack and a drink while they invite you to essentially eavesdrop, as we’ve all done, on a couple next to you. Tickets are $65 and include the show and 2 drinks.

Tuesday October 27

⭐ Dog-O-Ween Costume Contest
Leland Eating and Drinking House | 5-7pm at 755 Dean St, Prospect Heights

Leland’s dog-friendly patio hosts its annual Dog-O-Ween costume contest. Bring your dog in costume, or just come to watch other people’s dogs in costumes. There will be natural wine and Mediterranean snacks for you and pup-cups and treats for your pup, plus a heated patio with blankets if it gets chilly. I stumbled by totally by accident last year and they even had a red carpet. The real deal. No RSVP needed.

Special Feature: Hillbilly Allegedly

Picture the Monday night before the midterms. You’re in a basement on Clinton Street with a drink, everyone around you is a little feral from election dread, and JD Vance walks out to explain himself. Well technically comedian Dan Wilbur does, but he’s in character the entire time. The viral Vance impersonator has likely come across your feed and has been featured in The Onion, McSweeney’s, MTV, Funny or Die, The Today Show, and more. Tickets for the Nov 2nd show at Caveat are $19. Come along for some laughs.

A Few Good Men, Opening Night
Vivian Beaumont Theater | 7pm at 150 W 65th St, Lincoln Square

Aaron Sorkin's courtroom drama returns to Broadway in its first revival, directed by Michael Arden and starring Bradley Whitford, Tom Blyth, and Krysta Rodriguez. Military lawyer Daniel Kaffee is known for closing cases before trial, until defending two Marines accused of murder leads him to a cover-up and a collision with the chain of command. Runs through Jan 10. Tickets vary but are pricey.

Wednesday October 28

Le Dive East Pumpkin Carving Contest
Le Dive | 6-8pm at 37 Canal St, Lower East Side

Le Dive is throwing a Halloween Fest with a neighborhood pumpkin carving contest. Bring a pumpkin you’ve already carved to display and compete for the winning spot. Or just come have a glass of wine and see some of the creative submissions. No RSVP needed.

⭐ An Evening With The New York Times Op-Docs
IFC Center x New York Times | 6:30pm at 323 6th Ave, Greenwich Village

New York Times Op-Docs is hosting a screening of four of its award-winning short documentaries at the IFC Center. They will be followed by a Q&A with the filmmakers and the Op-Docs team. The line up includes La Retaguardia (four artists in Havana deciding whether to stay), Son (a mother communicating with her homeless son through his graffiti tags), Stalin Boys (four Texas middle schoolers with a Stalin fascination), and Living with a Visionary (a husband caring for his wife through vivid hallucinations after 50 years of marriage). Tickets are $20.

Bluefin Tuna Cutting Event
LUYA Omakase & Wine Bar | 5:30-8:30pm at 219 5th Ave, Park Slope

LUYA’s bluefin tuna cutting event returns. It’s a live whole bluefin tuna breakdown up close, then all-you-can-eat tuna for the rest of the evening. There will be sashimi, nigiri, and hand rolls, with toppings like uni, caviar, and truffle, from lean akami to rich toro. Tickets are $200.

Winter Village in Bryant Park also opens today. Go before all the tourists come to town.

Thursday October 29

⭐ Catholic Guilt
SoHo Playhouse | Through Nov 13th at 9pm at 15 Vandam St, SoHo

Kelly McCaughan brings her Edinburgh Fringe hit back to SoHo Playhouse for the New York Comedy Festival. It’s staged as a deranged, fractured church service in which McCaughan, who went to Catholic school from preschool through 12th grade, revisits the absurd experiences that shaped her understanding of just about everything: losing her virginity in the most holy way, abortion, a bowling experience that sent her straight to hell. Stand-up, clown, bouffon, and character work, with the audience pulled into the rituals. The show runs through Nov 13. Tickets are $40.

A Study in Collage and Layering
House of Three | 6-7pm at 13-15 W 28th St, NoMad

Popup Florist teams up with House of Three and ThirdLove to kick off the holiday season with an evening of making: one-of-a-kind collages and prints built from images, textures, and words that capture the people, places, and little things that make this time of year feel special. All materials are provided. Tickets are $10 and all proceeds go to the Lower Eastside Girls Club, an organization that connects young women of color throughout New York City to healthy and successful futures through free, innovative year-round programming and mentoring.

Dress Rehearsal
Union Hall | 7:30-9pm at 702 Union St, Park Slope

Dress Rehearsal is a comedy night where comedians try out new material in tuxedos, and the audience dresses up too. I like the concept. Haven’t heard of the comedians but feels like a fun new series to check out. Tickets are $15.

Friday October 30

⭐ John Donohue: Montreal Prints
L’Appartement 4F | Friday through Wednesday at 115 Montague St, Brooklyn Heights

Local painter and illustrator John Donohue, known for his hand-drawn restaurant facades, just got back from a painting trip to Montreal, and his gallery show of the trip’s prints takes over the French bakery from October 30 to November 5. The framed and canvas prints are for sale with all proceeds going to City Harvest. For the show, Normand Laprise, chef and co-owner of Montreal’s Restaurant Toqué!, teamed up with bakery owner Gautier Coiffard on a special wintergreen financier. The full collection runs to more than 50 drawings, viewable here. All prints are ~$250. This one hits home for me…literally. I grew up in Montreal and many of my favorite restaurants are featured.

Spiderwoman's Global Indigenous Theatre Festival
La MaMa | Through November 7 at 66 East 4th St, East Village

A nine-day festival celebrating 50 years of Spiderwoman Theater, the longest-running Native American women’s theatre company in the US. Founded in 1976 by sisters Muriel, Gloria, and Lisa Miguel, the company grew out of the feminist movement and became a leading voice for Indigenous women artists, building shows by weaving personal and traditional stories together with movement, music, and humor. The festival brings Indigenous artists from Australia, New Zealand, Canada, and Minneapolis to La MaMa, the East Village experimental theatre club dedicated to artists and all aspects of theatre-making. Check out their full schedule of shows.

Saturday October 31

Craftopia: DIY a Trick or Treat Tote
LeFrak Center at Lakeside, Prospect Park | 11am-4pm drop-in at Prospect Park

Fellow Substacker is bringing Craftopia to the Lakeside Fall Festival for a day of cozy, hands-on crafting. Oct 31 is tote day: grab a mini canvas tote and decorate it with scrap fabric and fabric markers, just in time to collect trick-or-treating treasures. All supplies are included, beginner friendly, and good for kids and your inner child. While you’re there, the festival has a haunted hotel, pumpkin patch, corn maze, and seasonal performances. Tickets are $15

Tim Burton After Dark: Halloween at W
W New York, Times Square | 8-11:30pm at 1567 Broadway, Midtown

W Times Square trades the typical Halloween party for a Tim Burton-inspired one. A fireside chat and Q&A with Jay Prychidny, Burton's longtime film editor (Beetlejuice, Beetlejuice and Wednesday), a live VFX artist building a fantastical creature through the night before its final reveal, Burton films projected all evening, a live DJ, a photobooth, and a costume contest. Your ticket includes a welcome glass of Perrier-Jouet plus an extra sip ticket. Tickets are $65.

Dumboween
Dumbo Archway | All day at Dumbo Archway

Dumbo's annual Halloween takeover is back. The highlight is their March to the Arch through Brooklyn Bridge Park with brass bands + puppets. There’s also Howl-O-Ween dog costume contest, crafts, live music, plus trick-or-treating at 60+ businesses. Spooky projections light up the Manhattan Bridge all week too. Free.

Halloween Bash: Ghosts of New York
Museum of the City of New York | 6-10pm at 1220 Fifth Ave, East Harlem

The museum’s annual Halloween Bash is back, and the dress code is the ghost of a famous New Yorker. Come for live tribute and drag performances by Mango, Tyrese Allums, Purss’ophonie, and Corma Kelley, costume contests with prizes for the best famous New Yorkers, themed cocktails at the Park View Bar, and DJ Misbehaviour on the South Terrace, plus an after-hours stroll through New York at Its Core and bites from local food vendors. Tickets are $20.

Sunday November 1

⭐ TCS New York City Marathon
TCS Marathon | All day all around the city

The best day of the year is back. More than 60,000 runners cover 26.2 miles from Staten Island through Brooklyn, Queens, and the Bronx to the finish on the east side of Central Park, in the 50th anniversary year of the five-borough course. I don’t care if you don’t know anyone running, finding a spot to post-up and cheer people on is required. I get weirdly emotional watching the city come together this way. Check out the course map to plan your stops. I usually post up along 4th Ave but I think I might try Williamsburg this year instead. Basically every restaurant and wine bar is having some sort of marathon party you can join.

Bracelet Making with Little Threads
Yu & Me Books | 2-4:30pm at 44 Mulberry St, Chinatown

A pop-up with Little Threads, a nonprofit bringing back bracelet making, so you can make a bracelet and re-experience a piece of childhood while giving back. All proceeds go to children's hospitals Little Threads partners with, including Mount Sinai and the Stony Brook pediatric hospital. RSVP for free.

Intimate Letters: A String Quartet Performance by the Met Chamber Ensemble
Poster House | 11am-1pm at 119 W 23rd St, Chelsea

A performance of Leoš Janáček's String Quartet No. 2, "Intimate Letters," presented in connection with the exhibition From Monarch to Modernity: Travel and Identity in the Czechoslovak First Republic, 1918-1938. Janáček wrote the quartet in 1928, inspired by his infatuation with Kamila Stösslová and the more than 700 letters he wrote her over the last decade of his life. The quartet is performed by violinists Sarah Vonsattel and Qianwen Shen, violist Tal First, and cellist Julia Bruskin, all members of the Metropolitan Opera Orchestra's Met Chamber Ensemble. Free with museum admission.

Dia de los Muertos Parade
New York Botanical Garden | 1-5pm at 2900 Southern Blvd, Fordham

The garden’s month-long Dia de los Muertos celebration closes with a parade. The afternoon starts with wearable art-making at 1pm, the procession itself at 2pm led by Son Pecadores musicians and dancers plus Mascara Viva’s giant La Catrina, skeleton, and monarch butterfly puppets, then a MAZarte folk dance performance at 2:30pm, a cumbia sonidera dance class at 3:15pm, and a dance party with food (churros, pan de muerto, tacos, tamales) through 5pm. The community altar is up all month if you want to add a photo or written memory of a loved one. RSVP for free.

What I did last week.

Places or shows I went to over the last week. These are personal recommendations. If I had a cool week, they’ll be cool. If I didn’t, they won’t.

  1. Hawksmoor - My husband woke up on the day before his birthday and requested Cote for dinner. I wasn’t quite able to make that reservation happen, but I took the hint that he wanted a steak and we ended up at Hawksmoor sharing a few different cuts and mushrooms that were so covered in cream they tasted more like mac n cheese. Still one of the most grand dining rooms in the city. They made us feel special by sending over dessert too.

  2. Radiant Cafe - A new favorite coffee shop. I got here 20 minutes early to meet a friend and was tempted by their chocolate croissant which ended up being one of the best I’ve had in the city. Great people watching and they keep it laptop free so it’s a great spot to meet someone and actually chat. It’s a wine bar at night which I’ll have to come back and try.

  3. Rooftop at Pier 17 - Ended up at yet another concert on the rooftop. This venue is incredible. I love that they never oversell it and that you can actually move. Plus the noise ordinance means concerts always end by 10pm. A dream.

  4. First We Bombed New Mexico - Saw this powerful documentary telling the story of a government betrayal with tragic consequences. It was followed by a Q&A with the filmmaker. It’s screening at the Angelika through October 31st.

item.title: Things to Do in NYC This Week (Oct 19 - Oct 25)
item.description: Come find me at the movies on Friday
item.dc:creator: Alexa Weiser
item.content:encoded:
My dog is scared of Halloween decorations. He growls at them, which I find endlessly funny. Our weekly Sunday long walk around Park Slope was twice as long as it usually is. We were following Park Slope Pulse’s spooky stoops map, which I highly recommend. I guess it was kind of mean of me to intentionally take him down the most decked out streets. But it was deeply wholesome to watch families pose in front of big pumpkins with their kids. Seriously, who thinks NYC has no neighborhood feel!?

The rest of the weekend was less wholesome and more just a lot. Open House New York plus every vintage fair and pop-up at once. One night I got home, dropped my bags, and had zero interest in the dinner reservation I’d made. My husband wanted to go out. A complete role reversal, and we laughed about being in each other’s shoes for once. We ended up going out.

I am exhausted. But as Anne Hathaway said, it’s fine to be tired if you like the reason you’re tired, and I really like my reasons. Lots of friends, food, and culture. My cup is full. Anyway, here’s everything worth leaving the house for this week.

Monday October 19

⭐ The Lebanese Table: Edy's Grocer x Sawa x Lebnani
Platform by JBF | 6:30pm at 25 11th Ave, Chelsea

A one-night-only multi-course Lebanese dinner celebrating the release of chef Jad Youssef's debut cookbook, Lebnani: A Journey Through Family, Food & the Flavours of Lebanon. Youssef and Aga Youssef, co-owners of Lebnani in Surrey, UK, join Edy Massih of Edy's Grocer and Samaya Boueri Ziade of Sawa for a cocktail reception with passed hors d'oeuvres, a multi-course menu with curated wine pairings, and a Q&A with the chefs. Tickets start at $185 and you can add on the book if you like.

Subscribe for the best things to do in NYC.

Juilliard Jazz Ensembles: Jazz Music of the 1970s
Dizzy's Club x Jazz at Lincoln Center | 7pm at Broadway at 60th Street, Lincoln Square

Two Juilliard ensembles, named for Betty Carter and Dizzy Gillespie, tackle the decade when jazz went modal, free-form, and avant-garde, through the music of Don Pullen, Charles Tolliver, John Hicks, and Thad Jones. The 7pm set is the Betty Carter Ensemble under Ben Wolfe, with the Dizzy Gillespie Ensemble following at 9pm. Tickets are $24.

Tuesday October 20

Screening: Friday the 13th
Deux Chats | 8:30pm at 27 Broadway, Williamsburg

Deux Chats, the South Williamsburg cocktail and oyster bar, is screening Friday the 13th as one of its film nights in an all-month October Halloween program. Popcorn is included. RSVP for free.

A Story of Gastronomy & Wine: Château Haut-Brion Library
Rizzoli Bookstore | 6pm at 1133 Broadway, NoMad

Pedro Corrêa do Lago celebrates his new book, a history of wine, gastronomy, and dining etiquette drawn from 150 rare documents in Château Haut-Brion’s culinary archive, in conversation with H.R.H. Prince Robert of Luxembourg, the man who runs the estate. A signing follows. RSVP for free.

It’s also Knicks Opening Night. There’s watch parties all around the city, but I’d go to your local bar instead of Hudson Yards or something.

Wednesday October 21

⭐ Jaywalker: New York Rye Whiskey Tasting
Jaywalker | 6-9pm at 573 Johnson Ave, Bushwick

Eleven New York distilleries, including Kings County, Taconic, and Fort Hamilton, pour under one roof for New York Rye Month at Jaywalker, the Brooklyn tasting room from the New York Distilling Company team. Tickets are $55 and include tastings from all the distilleries, a commemorative glass, a raffle entry, and first dibs on swag bags if you show up early.

Exceptional Hatred: Antisemitism and Free Speech in America, Past and Present
Center for Jewish History | 7-8:30pm at 15 W 16th St, Union Square

Historian James Loeffler joins New Yorker staff writer Emma Green for a conversation about antisemitism, free speech, and the challenges facing American democracy. Drawing on Loeffler's new book, they will explore why Jews and Israel so often stand at the center of debates over free expression, and how to confront hatred while protecting fundamental freedoms. Talk about a heavy topic. Registration for free.

What Season Is It, America?
Brooklyn Museum | Wednesday-Sunday from 11am-5pm at 200 Eastern Pkwy, Crown Heights

Artist Keith Yamashita fills the Beaux-Arts Court with a 250-foot circle of hundreds of poems, photographs, and pieces of Americana for 5 days only. You wander through, pick the works that resonate, and share your selections with the artist at a table. Sound artist Joshua Michéle Ross composes a new live score each day in response to the space. It's part of the museum's US@250 programming. I like that the installation asks you to actually participate instead of just look. Free with museum admission.

⭐ Art21's Big Night of Shorts
Powerhouse Arts | 7-9pm at 322 3rd Avenue, Gowanus

Art21's biennial screening night moves to the Gowanus fabrication hub, with short films from its Extended Play and New York Close Up series profiling Trey Abdella, Camille Henrot, Tishan Hsu, Arthur Jafa, Josh Kline, Precious Okoyomon, and Howardena Pindell. Several of the artists have fabricated work at Powerhouse, so the screening is something of a homecoming. A light reception follows the films. RSVP for free.

Thursday October 22

Bowl of 'Zole Brooklyn 2026
Industry City | 5-9pm at 33 35th St, Sunset Park

The pozole and agave spirits festival returns to Industry City with 20+ chefs serving pozole and classic Mexican dishes alongside 300+ pours of mezcal, tequila, raicilla, and sotol from artisan producers. It's all-inclusive: you build your own pairings and meet the chefs and producers behind them. Presented by Food Karma Projects with City Harvest, so some of the pozole goes to donation too.
Tickets are $65.

Speedboat Bar x The Otter
The Otter | Thursday-Saturday, seatings from 6pm at 58 Thompson St, SoHo

Luke Farrell's Speedboat Bar, the Thai-Chinese spot from the London team behind the Ambassadors Clubhouse (which I still can’t get into), cooks in the US for the first time with a three-night takeover of The Otter's back room. The menu sounds incredible. Tickets are $85 for the pre-set menu.

Candlelight Salon: An Evening of Music, Art & Connection
OPERA America | doors 8pm at 330 7th Ave (7th Floor), Chelsea

EastWest Artistry NYC's 45-minute fall artists showcase brings emerging vocalists and instrumentalists from Eastern and Western traditions to an intimate candlelit salon. The concert runs 8:15-9:00, and a meet-the-performers reception follows with snack and drink tastings included. Evening attire is encouraged which makes me even more intrigued. Tickets are $68.

Fianchetto: Social Chess
Barzakh Cafe | Thursday 6-8pm at 147 Utica Ave, Bed-Stuy

Fianchetto is a pop-up social chess club for all levels, boards provided, and Thursday's night lands at Barzakh Cafe. This is social chess, not competitive. You can show up, play a few games, meet some new people, and get a drink or small plate from the cafe. Tickets are $6.

Friday October 23

⭐ First We Bombed New Mexico – THE AFTERMATH
Village East by Angelika | Friday & Saturday at 7pm at 181-189 2nd Ave, East Village

Lois Lipman’s documentary follows Tina Cordova, a cancer survivor whose father was four when the first atomic bomb went off, through her 20-year fight for federal recognition of the Hispanic and Native families who lived downwind of the 1945 Trinity test in New Mexico. That fight ended with a 2025 law making the families eligible for compensation. Tina and Lois do live Q&As after the 7pm shows on Oct 23 and 24, and it’s an Oscar-qualifying run, so a strong opening weekend really matters for a small film like this. Tickets are $21. Come find me if you go on Friday.

⭐ The New Yorker Festival 2026
Various venues | All weekend in Manhattan

Three days of conversations, live podcast tapings, screenings, and music with the magazine's writers and editors. This year's lineup runs from Conan O'Brien with David Remnick and Gloria Steinem with Jia Tolentino to Aaron Sorkin, Ken Burns, Mahershala Ali, Ethan Hawke, Colson Whitehead, Min Jin Lee, Elizabeth Strout, and the Pixies with Amanda Petrusich. Since you’re actually reading this, hopefully you appreciate a magazine and think this is cool. Tickets vary in price, some are free! The main venues are Webster Hall, Joyce Theater, and T. Rowe Price Theatre.

Sprout n' Tell Showcase
Sprout Society | 7-10pm at 449 Troutman St, Bushwick

A night of music and art from Sprout Society, the Bushwick nonprofit running creative workshops for sober and sober-curious New Yorkers, with local artists hanging work on the show wall. You don't have to be sober to come, just open to a night out that isn't built around drinks. RSVP for free to see some cool art.

Saturday October 24

Taste of the Seaport
Piers 16 and 17 | 12-4pm at 89 South St, Seaport

The waterfront food festival is back after its September date got washed out by the nor'easter. Fifty downtown restaurants will have tastes for you, from Sadie's and Carne Mare to Le Gratin and Delmonico's, with chef demos and all. All proceeds go to the neighborhood's public schools. Eating well while funding public schools is pretty easy to say yes to. Tickets are $70 and get you six tastes. You get to choose which.

Longest Pastry Table
Driggs Ave | 11am-2pm, Williamsburg

One long pastry table set down the middle of Driggs Ave with a seat for every runner or non-runner ahead of the marathon next week. Organized by the North Brooklyn Parks Alliance, NBK Open Streets, and local run clubs, truly everyone is invited. Bring a pastry to share and partake in carb-loading. RSVP for free.

Seed Mixer
The Battery | 10am-12pm at the Sea Glass Carousel, Fidi

The Battery Conservancy's gardening team hosts a hands-on morning of collecting, cleaning, sorting, packaging, and sowing seeds, plus seed-bomb making, in the park's gardens. Some seeds feed the birds, some become next year's gardens, and there are seed-inspired bites. Free, all materials provided, family-friendly. A very wholesome way to spend a Saturday morning. Register for free.

A Legacy in Wine: The Family Cellar of Jannine and Robert MacDonnell
Sotheby's | 10am at 945 Madison Ave, Upper East Side

Sotheby's dedicates a live sale to the family cellar of Jannine and Robert MacDonnell, a single-owner collection built over decades with depth across Italy, Bordeaux, Burgundy, and the Rhone. Highlights include Richebourg 1999 from Domaine de la Romanee-Conti, a strong run of 2002 Burgundy from Rousseau, Dujac, and Emmanuel Rouget, and multiple case quantities of Comte Georges de Vogue's Musigny Cuvee Vieilles Vignes. These auctions are totally free to attend and I’d bet the people watching will be pretty good. No RSVP needed.

Trick or Treats: Bake Sale & Cafe
Kitsby Studio | 12-3pm at 393 Broadway, Tribeca

Kitsby turns its studio into a one-day Halloween bake sale and cafe with 13 NYC bakers bringing their spookiest treats, including Cakes by Lexi and her pumpkin spice sugar cookies which I’m particularly excited about. Kitsby will handle the cozy fall matcha and hojicha lattes too. Oh and costumes are welcome. Over 400 people have already RSVP'd, so the good stuff may not survive until 3pm. RSVP for free.

Sunday October 25

⭐ 5 Boro Foto Fest
Culture Lab LIC | 11am-6pm at 5-25 46th Ave, Long Island City

The first-ever 5 Boro Foto Fest, from The Phoblographer's Chris Gampat, is a one-day photography fair built around real, human-made, printed photography, with generative AI explicitly banned. More than 40 local photographers, galleries, and collectives exhibit and sell fine art prints, zines, books, and mixed media, indoors and out. Buy original work directly from the artists who made it. Register for free.

The Longest Table: Gowanus
Aligned NYC | 12-2pm at 1st & Bond, Gowanus

I guess every neighborhood has one of these now. The Longest Table, the community-potluck movement that started on a Chelsea street in 2022 and is now in 50+ cities, sets one long shared table down a Gowanus street canal. Bring food, drinks, or even decorations. RSVP for free and go ready to make friends.

Diwali Market
Tera Mera | 12-4pm at 272 Court St, Cobble Hill

The Cobble Hill Indian spot is hosting a Diwali market with local vendors selling candles, perfume, paan, jewelry, skincare, and sweets, plus live music, bracelet-making, and free henna from 1 to 4. Have lunch while you're there and make an afternoon of it. Free henna and paan in one afternoon is a pretty good Sunday.
See the vendor lineup.

What I did last week.

Places or shows I went to over the last week. These are personal recommendations. If I had a cool week, they’ll be cool. If I didn’t, they won’t.

  1. Tera Mera - This place is somehow my go-to Indian dinner and my go-to daytime cafe to chill and work at. I truly can’t think of any other space that does both day and night well. Plus, they serve their mango lassi in a champagne glass which made me feel fancy even though I wasn’t having a cocktail.

  2. Tera - No this is not a mistaken repeat. I was curious so looked up the difference in meaning between these 2 very similarly named restaurants. Tera Mera means “yours and mine” in Hindi and represents that food gets shared by everyone. Tera on the other hand is a Latin-derived concept meaning “of the earth”. Fun fact of the day. Anyway, I stumbled into Tera when trying to find literally anywhere to have a drink on the LES at 8pm on a Saturday with no reservation (impossible feat). I only had time to sit at their very well designed stone bar briefly, but I discovered that they’re known for their Tatami dinners and coffee omakases in the back room where there’s only 4 tables. I will definitely be back to try. Also a great spot to rent out for a 12 person dinner.

  3. Manhattan Vintage - I bought too much and I’m in trouble. I did a full deep dive if you want to see what I bought. Ignore what I spent.

  4. Machine Learning - I saw a new play that follows two couples hired to teach humanoid robots about human intimacy and I highly recommend you go before they close at the end of the month. The playwright, Kate Vozella, was kind enough to share a few words with me about her inspiration for the show which I’ve included in a bonus section below. Let me know if you like this kind of format so I can decide what to do more of. Also, like all the cool girls, Kate obviously has her own Substack where she has more reflections on what it means to be human. Follow along!

  5. Sunn’s - Wow wow wow. Probably in my top 5 meals of the year. A few friends and I met up with no plans and somehow snagged a spot walking into Sunn’s. Our waiter recommended we just get one of everything on the menu, so we did. We ended the meal fighting over our ranking of what was best. We decided it was everything. It’s just a plus that the space is so cozy too.

Interview with Playwright Kate Vozella

The show follows two couples hired to teach humanoid robots about human intimacy. Where did that premise start for you?

Kate: I wrote the first draft of this play in 2018, when the idea of humanoid companionship still felt like pure science fiction. I was interested in putting two romantic relationships under a microscope, or inside a pressure cooker, and seeing what might happen.

Romantic partnerships are endlessly fascinating to me. We all have ideas about how we want to love one another, how we want to behave, and what we want from love in return. But in practice, we so often fall short of those ideals. The characters in the play all want to be loved, but they struggle, in different ways, to love one another, or even to accept love when it’s offered.

And I started thinking: if we’re going to outsource love and intimacy to machines, how exactly are we going to teach them? Perhaps they’ll have to learn the way children do, by observing the relationships of their primary caregivers. But in doing so, we might inevitably pass on the same blind spots, insecurities and dysfunctional behaviors that we’ve inherited ourselves.

I suppose that’s what interested me most: the possibility that in trying to teach machines how to love, we might end up revealing just how little we understand about it ourselves.

The highlight of the show for me was how memorable the characters were. There were no cliches and you could feel their emotion. How do you write people that feel so realistic?

Thank you. What a lovely compliment! I’m sort of obsessive about rhythm in dialogue. I grew up in a chaotic household with a lot of noise, and I think that fine-tuned my ear for the details of conversation, especially in conflict: the little clues in cadence, the words people choose, or don’t choose, and the subtext sitting underneath it all.

But mostly, I just have a lot of fun writing conversations between people. That’s often how I begin a play, by writing and writing dialogue. Then, as I’m editing, I start to sculpt the characters. I might give a line to someone else, or tweak it slightly as the characters reveal themselves to me, until I feel confident that one person wouldn’t say something quite like that, but another would.

I also think it’s important not to shy away from “bad” behavior. I’m most interested in characters who exist somewhere between good and evil, between the moral and the immoral. That feels like a sweet spot of truth to me. People can be generous and selfish, loving and cruel, sometimes within the same conversation. I don’t particularly want to make excuses for my characters or condemn them. I’m more interested in understanding how they arrive at their choices, even when those choices are difficult to defend. I think that’s often where they begin to feel most human.

I spent my subway ride home thinking about what makes humans “human”. What are the discussions or questions you hope the audience has on the way home? Did I get it right?

ooo yes, what a huge and impossible question to answer, but it’s definitely the right question to be asking (I think). I’m very interested in what makes us human, particularly as technology begins to imitate more and more of the things we’ve historically considered uniquely ours. Is it our capacity for love, empathy, imagination? Or is it also our irrationality, our cruelty, our inability to understand ourselves and one another?

I suppose I’m less interested in arriving at a definitive answer than in complicating the question. We tend to talk about humanity as though it’s something inherently good, something we need to preserve or protect. But being human is also messy, contradictory, and sometimes quite ugly. If we’re going to build machines in our image, we might have to confront some uncomfortable truths about the image we’re reproducing.

item.title: Day 1 at Manhattan Vintage
item.description: I bought so much my bag broke
item.dc:creator: Alexa Weiser
item.content:encoded:
Manhattan Vintage, the show where I found my wedding dress, is back this weekend. More on that in my vintage in NYC guide from this summer.

I went in yesterday with high expectations. Not that I was worried, but it did not disappoint.

Here’s how the day went: what I tried, what I bought, and what I left behind.

My weekend started with a Thursday night panel with three vintage icons, a free talk at the Museum at FIT. Their talks are always free and truly no one I speak to knows about them, despite the lineup being incredible. They fill up quickly so it's worth keeping an eye on the speaker list. And no, it's not students; I think I was the youngest person there. Hearing people I'd known of speak so passionately about vintage and personal style left me in awe of them, and it reinvigorated this obsession with fashion I've always had. I made myself a goal: take a picture of my outfit before I'm out the door, every single day for a year. I dress for myself and my mood more than the occasion, but this will force me to play with what's in my closet and chase that rush when I know I nailed it. Beyond the outfits themselves, I want to spend more time covering fashion news and events in the city. Writing the guide earlier this year was one of the most fun pieces I've done, and while it's not my core niche, I want more of it. Starting here.

Now to the panel itself. First, Vogue editor and fashion historian Lilah Ramzi. I mistook her for Anne Hathaway for a moment. She was one of the most put-together people I've encountered; she spoke about and showed pictures of pieces she loves going back to the 40s and 50s. I went down a hole stalking her after the talk, admittedly jealous of all the black-tie occasions, ballets and the like, where she gets to wear fabulous gowns and coats. I hate catching myself holding back on a purchase I love for lack of occasion, and I aspire to a calendar that no longer makes me question that. Her Vogue piece tracing the origin of the vintage dress she found for her wedding resonated strongly. I'm on a similar, though far less dedicated, mission myself. She also asserted something I've known to be true but that makes vintage shopping harder: it's sacrilegious to separate a set.

Subscribe now

Next, stylist Danny Santiago. He should be in some hall of fame or something. I guess doing costume design for Sex and the City and Confessions of a Shopaholic is kind of as good as it gets. He apparently has a warehouse with moving dry-cleaner racks to house his collection. If anyone can get me a visit, I'll love you forever.

And finally Amy Abrams, owner of the Manhattan Vintage show, which is just one of her ventures. She’s living the dream (or my dream), running it with her husband as her partner and bringing dealers and artists to the people. She started Artists and Fleas nearly 25 years ago, now huge across Williamsburg and Chelsea, and runs the show that inspired this post. Something she said stuck with me: when asked what piece she goes in looking for, she said she intentionally doesn’t focus on finding something specific. She looks for whatever speaks to her in the moment. Over the years I’ve changed how I shop, from “I want a Fendi baguette” to yesterday, where I was just there for whatever caught my eye and whatever fabric I couldn’t stop touching.

Quite the panel indeed.

How Day 1 went

I was first in line and got to skip the already-forming line as press. As usual I was overwhelmed the second I walked in, but I’ve learned from my mistakes and beelined for the back corner booth. It’s easy to get stuck in the entryway crowd, and I wanted to take advantage of being nearly alone, which lasted about ten minutes.

I made my first purchase in those ten minutes. I usually do a full round, note the booths, and circle back to the pieces I photographed. Taking something to the changing rooms kills too much time before I’m sure it’s the one. But this booth (Aric Studio, which I now follow) had a mini curtain changing room inside it (a rarity!). The dress (silk paired with intricate beading) fell on me perfectly and the two-tone navy and purple matches a pair of slingbacks I already own. I knew I was buying her before I’d even zipped her up.

Purchase #1: Beaded bodice dress over a navy silk skirt; $118.95 (a steal too)

Next I passed a booth with two cardigans, one Versace, one Escada, that made the picture list but didn’t come home with me. Looking at the Escada now, a cream mohair cardigan with a black curly collar and black trim, I’m regretting it. I wonder if it’s still there. No picture, partly because it’s blurry, partly because I’m running back for her.

Year over year, I’m less drawn to name-brand purses. I guess I’m taking Amy’s advice and gravitating toward what actually makes me feel something. This late-80s satin clutch with the floral pattern did just that. If it fit my phone, it would have been purchase #2.

Next, Cavalli. The sexiest dress that exists. I tried her on but the straps were way too long. No picture of her on me because she was halfway down my chest.

I was due for a pop of color after all that darkness. I think Pierre Cardin is severely underrated today. The shoulder pads were too much for my frame, unfortunately, but the canary yellow silk blouse with the faint croc texture was hard to leave behind. My hat is a bit much with it, but I even like it with the skirt I happened to be wearing.

We don’t wear enough men’s clothes. I don’t mean men’s-inspired clothing or the oversized power suit trend. I mean literal vintage men’s clothes. I’d love to meet more men’s-focused dealers, whether sourcing for men (does anyone do it well?) or just carrying men’s pieces women can wear. I tried on a men’s grey speckled tweed waistcoat with matching trousers (turned up about six times at the hem, but the waist fit). I’d wear them as separates. I left it behind. It was a bit itchy and I’m sensitive to that, but I liked the idea.

I’m a sucker for any accessory that matches my current outfit, which led to purchase #2. This lapis bead necklace with jade and an enamel bird pendant caught my eye. I turned it over and saw the other side of the pendant was a dragon, which sealed it.

Purchase #2: Lapis bead necklace with pendant; $148

A Saint Laurent blouse and skirt set caught my eye next. The dusty rose dot print was so beautiful and I love a good button. Sadly, too big.

Purchases #3 and #4 came in quick succession from the same vendor, who’d come in from London. I’d been circling the booth too overwhelmed to decide what to grab for the dressing room. About twelve people were in there; things were going fast and it was physically hard to move. I think I chose right though.

Purchase #3: Olive silk gown from the 30s; $1,200

Purchase #4: Cropped tuxedo blazer with gold and red dragon embroidery; $800

This same booth (One Vintage Designs) had so much else that was hard to pass up, notably a Dries Van Noten open jacket, a Lanvin gold beaded slip dress, and a black sleeveless maxi with embroidered flowers. But I had to keep moving.

I tried on a burgundy and gold geometric print blouse (Etro or Escada, I can’t quite remember) but couldn’t justify the price. Kept moving.

Next to catch my eye: a 70s Saks Fifth Avenue corset belt. It was textured like a painting. Still thinking about it and wishing I’d tried it on.

The back row of the show is all coats. I actually need a leather jacket, but of course I tried on everything except that. I put on about twelve green-tone overcoats, mostly wool. Some pictured here. None fit quite right, so I kept moving.

The bag collection was to die for. An entire wall of Baguettes, including the embellished denim ones, my personal favorites. But after stealing one of my mom’s statement Baguettes ahead of my wedding, I can’t justify another. They weren’t incredibly priced either. Other vendors had plenty of Chanel flaps, leather Bottega, and more.

And finally, my last purchase. I was quite literally dropping from shopping, a saying I didn’t understand until yesterday, lugging my laptop and too many bags around for hours. I knew the next thing I found would be my last. My wallet was also feeling loose. A cropped boxy Dries Van Noten jacket it was. (My first Dries piece eeeeek!). I know I’ll throw it on constantly. I wore it to grab a casual bite last night, getting some wear in immediately.

Purchase #5: Dries jacket; $550

What a day. I can’t wait to style every piece this fall. What I love most about vintage is pairing it with non-vintage to make a look. At this point most of my outfits have at least one vintage component (thanks in large part to the pieces my mom is very slowly parting with). They elevate a look in a way I can’t explain. And I love chasing down the exact era and story of a piece. I threw this together too quickly to finish my research, but I’ll be following up with everything I find.

Happy shopping! The show runs through Sunday. Run. And if you see me, implore me to have some self-control.
