item.title: Things to Do in NYC This Week (Oct 12 - Oct 18)
item.description: Three dog parades in a single Saturday
item.dc:creator: Alexa Weiser
item.content:encoded:
I went to the Morning Market series at Union Square Cafe last week. We chatted over breakfast, and even had some breakfast wine, before taking a stroll through the Greenmarket. I also got to meet and , two Substackers I love who also write about New York. It was fun to trade notes and hear more about how they put their letters together. Talking to two people who do this for real sent me straight back to the daydream I have every few months about doing the letter full time. It's getting harder to shelve the thought entirely.

I realized something else while I was there: almost everything in this newsletter happens after traditional work hours, because I assume that’s when you’re free. But there’s so much good stuff going on during the workday too. Let me know if I should start including more of it.

Special Feature: Sixpenny Presents Daydream

I’m thrilled to have Sixpenny sponsoring this issue of City Happenings. I've had my eye on them since I first saw their slipcovered sofa in a friend's Fort Greene apartment.

For one day only, they’re popping up with an immersive, whimsical installation at Elizabeth Street Garden. DAYDREAM brings Sixpenny's new fabric colors to life on fresh and familiar pieces in a “fantastical tapestry of botanical theater”. Swing by from 11am-6pm on Saturday to see the collection. Keep an eye on the event page for a reschedule in case of rain. I snuck in a preview of the new fabric colors further down so you can take a peak.

Monday October 12

Rediscovering the Northeast’s Forgotten Crops
Farm.One | 6pm at 625 Bergen St, Prospect Heights

An evening at Brooklyn’s indoor vertical farm celebrating climate-adaptive perennial crops of the Northeast, with blackcurrants and tree nuts as the headliners. You’ll hear from two brands that are working to build the market for these crops and then mingle and samples the products. Tickets are $30 and include a drink.

Subscribe for the best things to do in NYC.

Jeepers Creepers (35mm)
Nitehawk Cinema x Romeo’s | 6:30pm at 136 Metropolitan Ave, Williamsburg

Jeepers Creepers is getting a full Nitehawk treatment: 35mm, a pre-party at Romeo’s (the neon-lit 90s cocktail den in the East Village) with themed drinks from 6:30-8:30pm, a special Romeo’s cocktail collaboration during the screening, and an after-party in Lo-Res. Pretty rare to see an event span two boroughs. Tickets are $15.

Drawing From Art: Iceland
Scandinavia House | 5:30pm at 58 Park Ave, Murray Hill

A hands-on drawing workshop with New York artist Charity Baker focused on Icelandic art, part of her six-session series at Scandinavia House. Each session pairs a 30-minute overview of celebrated Nordic artists with 1.5 hours of drawing directly from the works in graphite, charcoal, ink, or colored pencil, with all materials provided, no experience necessary. Tickets are $35.

Tuesday October 13

⭐ Building New York: How the New Deal Transformed the City
The General Society Library | 6-7:30pm at 20 W 44th St, Midtown

Architectural historian Matt Postal, of the Art Deco Society of New York, gives an illustrated talk on how FDR’s New Deal funneled federal dollars to Fiorello LaGuardia and Robert Moses, who remade all five boroughs with housing, hospitals, schools, parks, pools, bridges, and public art. It’s at the General Society Library, whose lecture series dates to 1837. Tickets are $15.

40th Anniversary Gala: En Garde Arts
En Garde Arts | 6:30pm at 509 Atlantic Ave, Boerum Hill

For site-specific theater company En Garde Arts’ 40th anniversary, they’re throwing a fundraiser gala. Over the years they’ve created performances in the places where this city lives from streets and stoops to living rooms. Basically wherever New Yorkers gather. The evening starts with cocktail hour, then the world premiere of Bogart and Mee's new outdoor work Prelude, then a literal processional to Roulette for the gala celebration, with Sarah Gancher, Hansol Jung, Jared Mezzocchi, and more artists in the room. Tickets start at $150.

Books and Bites: Don't Think About Dinner
Platform by JBF | 6pm at Pier 57, Chelsea

NYT bestselling author and viral food personality Jenn Lueke (@jenneatsgoood) sits down with TODAY food stylist Krissy Downey to talk her debut cookbook, Don't Think About Dinner. It’s 125+ easy, nourishing recipes for every meal, framed as the cure for weeknight decision fatigue. Bites come straight from the book's pages, and copies will be available to buy from Kitchen Arts & Letters. Tickets are $45.

Wednesday October 14

Queens Climate Night
Our House | 7-8pm at 23-71 31st St, Astoria

Our House, a co-working space in Astoria, is hosting a neighbor-led evening of learning about climate topics and taking meaningful action toward a just, livable future. No RSVP needed, just show up!

Bhangra in the Plaza
34th Street Partnership | 6pm at Greeley Square Plaza, Midtown

A free outdoor bhangra lesson in the middle of Midtown, led by Sarina Jain and dancers from Masala Bhangra. Bhangra is the high-energy Punjabi folk dance, and here you watch and learn choreography set to contemporary Indian music, with all ages and experience levels welcome. The free outdoor dancing events in NYC were some of my favorites of the summer. Glad to see we still have a couple this fall. RSVP for free.

Thursday October 15

Food for Thought 2026: A Celebration of Food, Community, and Opportunity
Prospect Park Picnic House | 6pm at 40 West Dr, Park Slope

The Park Slope Civic Council's signature annual tasting event returns to the Picnic House, with bites and pours from roughly two dozen local spots (Winner, Palo Santo, Lore, Scottadito, Dram Shop, and plenty more). Every ticket funds scholarships for graduating seniors at the John Jay Educational Campus, and this year's event honors Rasheed Rankine, a John Jay grad turned college counselor. I love a neighborhood tasting where the ticket doubles as a donation. Tickets are $100.

Salon Creatives
Casa La Femme | 6:30pm at 140 Charles St, West Village

Salon Creatives is an (un)professional gathering for working, aspiring, and self-proclaimed creatives in New York City. The goal is to bring people together to find a collaborator, a friend, or a tool you haven’t heard of yet. It’ll be a mix of professional and amateur filmmakers, musicians, artists, and more. RSVP for free.

⭐ Produce Parties Carrot Party
TALEA Beer Co | 7pm at 87 Richardson St, Williamsburg

Produce Parties, the ingredient-themed potluck series, is throwing its second Carrot Party at TALEA's Williamsburg taproom, and there is exactly one rule: bring a carrot dish to share. They’re partnering in carrot with Brami, Marianne's, and San Pellegrino. There will be a Carrot Spritz made with San Pellegrino, archival magazines for sale, a seasonal t-shirt drop, and a free gift bag from partners Brami, Marianne's, and San Pellegrino. Tickets are $37.

Friday October 16

⭐ Open House New York Weekend
Open House New York | Oct 16-18, all five boroughs

The annual architecture-and-infrastructure festival unlocks 300+ destinations across all five boroughs for behind-the-scenes tours, talks, and more. This year's lineup includes Roy Lichtenstein's former studio, a 1929 Bronx movie palace, an active subway construction site, hidden Rockefeller Center gardens, a working power plant, and basically any niche New York thing you’re curious to get an inside look at. Most sites are drop-in and free. Tickets are needed for others, check out the full schedule. It’s one of my favorite weekends of the year (closely behind NYC Marathon weekend) so I also wrote a deep dive on some of the spots I’m most excited to get an inside look at.

⭐ BRIC JazzFest
BRIC House | 6pm Friday & Saturday at 647 Fulton St, Downtown Brooklyn

Night 1 of the two-night jazz festival from BRIC, the downtown Brooklyn arts nonprofit, takes over all three stages at BRIC House with Bilal, Arturo O'Farrill and the Afro Latin Jazz Orchestra paying tribute to Randy Weston, plus Marcus Gilmore, Takuya Kuroda, Sparklmami, and Laura Anglade. This year's curatorial theme is "Radical Joy". It’s a fun format with performances running simultaneously across rooms, so you can drift between them with a drink. Tickets start at $62.

MasterZ at Work Dance Family: The 24/7 Diner
Free Food Refettorio Harlem | 5:15pm at 37 W 119th St, Harlem

Works & Process (the performing arts organization that commissions work and presents at the Guggenheim) is doing free pop-up performances at Refettorio Harlem, the city's only free restaurant (a Massimo Bottura Food for Soul project serving vulnerable neighbors). First, a gourmet sit-down dinner from 5:15-6:45pm, then at 5:45pm a performance of The 24/7 Diner, a new ballroom-rooted work by choreographer Courtney "Balenciaga" Washington about chosen family and joy as resistance. A free sit-down dinner and a commissioned dance premiere on a Friday night is a pretty good deal. Register here.

⭐ Manhattan Vintage Fall 2026 Show
Metropolitan Pavilion | Oct 16-18 at 125 West 18th Street, Chelsea

Ninety vintage dealers take over the Metropolitan Pavilion for three days of curated secondhand shopping. Tickets are $25. If you’ve been following along for a while, you know this is my top pick for vintage shopping in the city. I never miss a show. More on my vintage favorites in my guide from this summer.

Strange & Beautiful: A Writing Salon on the Inexpressible
Dilly Dally | 6:30-9pm at 626 Vanderbilt Ave, Prospect Heights

Lit Society's guided salon takes on "literary difficulty" with writing instructor Hank Jost, working through excerpts from Shakespeare, Joyce, Melville, Virginia Woolf, and more to figure out what makes a sentence feel dense, strange, or beautiful. Then you turn the tools on your own writing, with exercises starting from sound and nonsense and building toward voice, rhythm, and syntax. No prior writing experience is needed. Tickets are $125 and include a cocktail and light bites.

Saturday October 17

The Halloween Dog Parade Tripleheader
All over the city | East Village, Carroll Gardens, Coney Island

Three separate costumed dog parades are happening on the same Saturday. Truly only in New York. You can technically make a day of it and go to all three.

  • Tompkins Square Halloween Dog Parade (11am, Tompkins Square Park along Avenue B): the big one, back for its 36th year with thousands of costumed dogs, presented by Kismet and produced by the New York Dog Parade nonprofit. Festival block with photo ops, sponsor activations, and an ASPCA adoptable-dog spotlight for Adopt a Shelter Dog Month. Free to watch; marching dogs need advance registration at NYDogParade.org, first-come first-served.

  • Howl-O-Ween Red Carpet Dog Parade (3-5pm, Smith St at Union St): the inaugural edition, from MOSS (the Merchants of Smith Street) and Pupstarz Rescue as part of the Neighbors & Makers Street Fair. Dogs strut a red carpet emceed by Freddie Fox & Trixie Rose, with free doggie gift bags for the first 30 signups. RSVP for free.

  • Boo on the Boardwalk (1-4pm, Coney Island Boardwalk from W 10th St to Stillwell Ave): the Coney Island BID’s trick-or-treat setup with Boo Stops, face painting, and costume contests for kids and pets. Free.

⭐ Brownstone Boys Stoop Sale No. 3
The Brownstone Boys Studio | 10am-2pm at 375 Vanderbilt Ave, Clinton Hill

The Brownstone Boys, the Instagram-famous renovation duo, are opening their Clinton Hill carriage house for the third annual stoop sale with their best vendor lineup yet: Drake Vaccaro's florals, Brooklyn Vintage Company, Small Things Studios ceramics, Petunia Jewelry, FAULT New York, and a half dozen more vintage dealers and makers, plus pieces from the boys' own collection of renovation leftovers. Red Jacket Orchards is pouring hot apple cider, and paid subscribers to their Substack get 10% off everything. No RSVP needed, check out the full list of vendors.

Reminder to check out the Sixpenny pop up at Elizabeth Street Garden. The previews of their new fabric colors are incredible.

Sunday October 18

Furniture & Decor Fair
BQ Flea | 10am-5pm at 202 Meeker Ave, Williamsburg

Brooklyn Flea's under-the-BQE Sunday market is running a special Furniture & Decor Fair edition with bigger statement pieces and one-of-a-kind home furnishings instead of the usual smalls. Think mid-century credenzas, vintage lounge chairs, handmade ceramics, framed art, and eclectic decor, all in the concrete expanse under the expressway. No RSVP needed.

⭐ Threes Flea by Fig Shop
Threes Brewing | 12-7pm at 113 Franklin St, Greenpoint

Fig Shop, the vintage shop behind the FIG Flea pop-up markets, is curating another edition of the flea at Threes Brewing. There will be local vendors selling art, vintage, books, and records, with a DJ set in the afternoon. Food by Grand Army and drinks by Threes Brewing are available. RSVP for free.

La MaMa 65th Anniversary Block Party
La MaMa | 1-5pm on E 4th St between Bowery and Second Ave, East Village

La MaMa, the legendary East Village experimental theater, turns 65 with a free block party on Ellen Stewart Way, built around the theme "Art for Healing, Food for Healing". Performances run from Brooklyn United to Tibetan singer Yungchen Lhamo, DJ Blanka Barbara, and the Great Jones Repertory Company, with family activities like puppet making, kids yoga, and a bouncy house in the mix. Local spots including Paul's Da Burger Joint and Bar Monto are handling the food. RSVP for free.

What I did last week.

Places or shows I went to over the last week. These are personal recommendations. If I had a cool week, they’ll be cool. If I didn’t, they won’t.

  1. Morning Market Series at Union Square Cafe - I’ve featured this series before and with good reason. Union Square Cafe brings in a chef from another New York institution (this time Anthony Mangieri of Una Pizza) to host a conversation about their culinary world. We chatted over breakfast, and even some breakfast wine, before taking a stroll through the Union Square Greenmarket. I believe they’re hosting the last one for the season in a few weeks with guest Alison Roman.

  2. Great Job News - I went to the debut screening of this news(ish) show. It was far more entertaining and far less anxiety inducing than the actual news. Two comedians host the show which doesn’t hurt. I had so much fun I even posted a story from the event on my ~new~ Instagram. I literally have dozens of followers if you’d like to be part of the exclusive club.

  3. Caputo Bagels - When a new bagel shop opens within a few blocks from me, it’s pretty much a guarantee I’m going week 1. I seem to have made it before the inevitable crowds. It was also a Tuesday which may have helped. I had an everything bagel for cream cheese and the sourdough bagel was incredible. I’m excited to go back and try their eggplant bagel sandwich (new for me, but hey it caught my eye).

  4. Littlefield - Discovered this independent live venue in Gowanus at an event last week and have since gotten really excited about their line up this fall. They have a mix of comedy, variety shows, screenings, and more. It just feels very neighborhood-y and and intimate.

item.title: The City Happenings Draft #2: Art World
item.description: We mapped the art scene in NYC
item.dc:creator: Alexa Weiser
item.content:encoded:
The City Happenings Draft

Every corner of New York has its own experts, regulars, and strong opinions. In this series, I invite someone deeply immersed in a niche to draft their ideal version of that world with me. We take turns claiming the places, events, and experiences we’d choose first, and once something’s picked, it’s off the board.

New York’s art world extends far beyond the big-name museums. There are gallery openings, public installations, emerging artist studios, and communities that form around them all.

To help map the scene, I teamed up with Sarah, the creator of , a newsletter (and forthcoming speaker series) that wants you to see more art in the city.

Rather than making a list of recommendations, we held a draft across 8 art-adjacent categories.

  1. Museum – One museum you never miss.

  2. Gallery – One gallery whose programming you’d follow all year.

  3. Neighborhood for Art – Chelsea, Lower East Side, Tribeca, Bushwick, Upper East Side, etc.

  4. Drink or Snack After a Show – Best place for a drink after seeing a show.

  5. Recent Opening – A show or space everyone should experience.

  6. Emerging Artist Discovery Spot – The place you go to find artists before everyone else.

  7. Place to Learn About Art – Lectures, educational organizations, tours, critiques, classes.

  8. Wildcard – Anything art-adjacent.

The rules are simple. We alternate picks in a snake draft format. Once a category is taken, it’s off the board. This means only one of us gets to claim the city’s best museum, gallery, public art piece, etc. By the end, we’ll each have assembled half of our ideal art world in New York.

Let's get into it.

Alexa: You’re the guest here, so I’ll let you kick things off.

Pick 1: Museum

Sarah drafts: The Morgan Library

Longtime subscribers probably won’t be surprised by this but it’s The Morgan Library. They’ve never sent me a press email, and I am there pretty reliably covering it. Smaller museums – like The Guggenheim – are usually a tougher sell too because, if you don’t like the show you came for, there isn’t a giant permanent collection you can peruse to not feel like you wasted your ticket. It’s much harder for smaller venues to be consistently worthwhile.

Alexa: Great pick. I sometimes go just to sit in the quiet and read. It’s worth the admission for that alone.

Pick 2: Gallery

Alexa drafts: Artists Space

I was tempted to just take the easy win here with a Zwirner or a Gagosian or something. But visiting those sometimes feel more like walking through a museum. I wanted to go for something with a bit more character.

Artists Space has been around since 1972, and it’s spent that whole time supporting artists outside the commercial system entirely. It’s now in a genuinely beautiful home in Tribeca (8,000 square feet across two floors!) and they also run a dedicated performance program of music, readings, and more. I always keep an eye on their calendar.

Sarah: I don’t know much about Artists Space, but I take your point that it’s worth having a list of places that are decidedly not in the Zwirner/Gagosian camp. The one art neighborhood that I think is bustling with this sentiment right now is Ridgewood. I’ve been starting to make some pilgrimages out there.

Subscribe now

Pick 3: Emerging Artist Discovery Spot

Sarah drafts: Trust your preferred galleries

As someone trying to build an independent arts media brand, I don’t really chat too much with galleries. It’s important to me that Exhibits in New York remains a place that can publish negative reviews. I am also VERY friendly in person and would probably find it hard to maintain editorial independence if I was socializing too much with that side of the art world. That said, I do respect that a gallery’s whole job is to find and nurture emerging talent. I think you should use your feet and walk around this city and note when you find a space that is consistently putting on shows you like. Whoever they pick as an emerging artist is probably someone you should watch. I’m also going to take this moment to sneak in one of my gallery picks in the city which is Ulrik in Chinatown.

Alexa: The surrendering-editorial-independence bit hit home. I try to be disciplined about the openings and restaurant events I say yes to. I don’t want to write something negative in my reviews but I want to stay authentic. I’ve never been to Ulrik. I’ll have to check it out!

Pick 4: Place to Learn About Art

Alexa drafts: Dia Art Foundation

Most “learn about art” options end up being dry lectures or Instagram-bait “immersive experiences”. Dia is neither. Their Dia Talks series has had people like Antoine Catala speaking on Donald Judd, or Evelyn Taocheng Wang on Agnes Martin. You’re hearing from someone who actually makes things and it makes a real difference in tone.

They also run free public tours most Saturdays, led by practicing artists. I’ve more than once ended up in a real conversation with the guide about something I clearly didn’t understand. Despite often being the least knowledgeable person in the room, they never make me feel that way. And everything’s free, always.

Sarah: Yeah I think we’re headed to a real boom in ways we’ll learn about art. I will say that my preferred way is to read as many old exhibition reviews as possible. You’d be surprised by how much more useful those contemporaneous reactions are relative to what gets written in later biographies and catalogs. Read everything you can in The New Yorker’s archive. Read as many old reviews from The Village Voice you can get your hands on.

Pick 5: Drink or Snack After a Show

Sarah drafts: The Bar Room at the Modern

I try not to eat out when I’m going to shows as that leads to somewhere financially irresponsible. That said, I am a sucker for getting a drink at a comfortable spot to unpack my thoughts after a show, especially if I know I want to review it. I will have a glass of wine at The Bar Room at the Modern if I’m at MoMA or Galerie Buchholz. I’m on a real off-dry riesling kick right now. Hav & Mar is where I stop for a breather if I’m doing a busy night of Chelsea openings.

Alexa: I never learn. I’m definitely in the camp of forgetting to eat, walking way too much, and then overpaying for something mediocre. I need to pre-stuff my purses with snacks. The Modern is great. They have a ton of pop ups with local restaurants too so I always keep an eye on their calendar.

Pick 6: Neighborhood for Art

Alexa drafts: Lower East Side

I’ll take the Lower East Side over Chelsea any day. The galleries are smaller and weirder in a great way.You get real range in a few blocks: a place like James Fuentes or Company Gallery next door to something you’ve never heard of and never will again after this show closes. The unpredictability is kind of the whole appeal to me.

Case in point: back in the spring, I saw some lights on and a small crowd and wandered into what I assumed was a gallery after finishing a day of shopping. It turned out to be part art opening, part vinyl pop-up bar, and I ended up on the back patio for a few glasses of wine before I fully understood what I was at. I’ve tried to retrace my steps more than once since. I still couldn’t tell you where it was.

Sarah: A perfect day. I’m a real believer in serendipity. You have to let random things happen to you. I know everyone wants to have a gallery day mapped out, but I see shows by just picking one and then meandering around. Ask the people who work at galleries what nearby shows they’re passionate about. Ask them what they think isn’t any good. You will have a better time that way, I promise.

Pick 7: Recent Opening

Sarah drafts: The Studio Museum

The Studio Museum in Harlem just opened their Artist in Residence exhibition featuring Derriann Pharr, Simonette Quamina, and Taylor Simmons. I remember last year, when the Studio Museum re-opened, they did a show of work from nearly everyone who had participated in the artists-in-residence program since it started in 1968. You really got a sense of how many important people came through that program–artists like Kerry James Marshall, Valerie Maynard, and David Hammons. Jennifer Packer is a personal favorite. I’m not sure it was my favorite exhibition during the re-opening, but it was the one that felt most like the museum’s mission statement.

Alexa: Another new one for me! I’ve already got a few Apollo shows on the calendar this fall and it’s right down the street, so a full culture day is clearly in order.

Pick 8: Wildcard

Alexa drafts: Pioneer Works

This is my wildcard because Pioneer Works isn’t really a gallery or a museum. It’s a nonprofit cultural center in Red Hook that blends art, science, and music in a way I haven’t found anywhere else in the city. It’s housed in a restored 19th-century ironworks building, with three floors of studios, labs, and performance space, and even a garden out back.

The reason it made my board over an actual gallery is really its Second Sundays programming. It’s a free monthly open house where their artists-in-residence open their studios. There’s live music, workshops, and food trucks scattered across the whole campus. There’s always something new and unexpected and unlike much of the art world, it’s approachable and unpretentious.

Sarah: I live near Pioneer Works, and it arguably gets outsized coverage from me because of that. They also have one of my favorite literary events of the year. I love Red Hook–it’s the city’s most Philadelphian neighborhood (complimentary).

Final Rosters

Sarah’s art world

  1. The Morgan Library (Museum)

  2. Trust your preferred galleries (Emerging Artist Discovery Spot)

  3. Bar Room at the Modern (Snack After a Show)

  4. The Studio Museum (Recent Opening)

Alexa’s art world

  1. Artists Space (Gallery)

  2. Dia Art Foundation (Place to Learn About Art)

  3. Lower East Side (Neighborhood for Art)

  4. Pioneer Works (Wildcard)

Alexa: This was fun! Thanks for taking part in the series. Do you have any final art world recommendations to leave us with?

Sarah: On the drinks/snacks point, I just went to Terroir in Tribeca. You shouldn’t go there if you’re solo and wanting to think critically about the art you saw, but if you have a group of friends doing a Tribeca gallery crawl and end up there for drinks after, you’ll have a good time. Very casual, can get loud, but has a killer wine list. My day job is in wine–it’s kind of an industry spot.

item.title: Things to Do in NYC This Week (Oct 5 - Oct 11)
item.description: City Happenings gets a makeover
item.dc:creator: Alexa Weiser
item.content:encoded:
City Happenings is very slowly developing what I believe the professionals call a brand identity.

It recently occurred to me that after more than two years of sending this newsletter, I could perhaps use a font other than the default one. Or have an actual email banner. To be clear, my fonts have not been updated yet, but I’m starting to give the letter a bit of a makeover.

You can see a small preview of it today, and I’ll be playing around with the design over the next week or so. Nothing too dramatic (I’m quite literally not capable), but hopefully soon you’ll be able to recognize a City Happenings letter before actually reading it.

Monday October 5

⭐ News & Brews #2: Prediction Markets
Crystal Lake Brooklyn | 6:30-8:30pm at 647 Grand St, Williamsburg

Newsreel's phone-free night of drinking and arguing about the news returns with a live question: are prediction markets a better way to report uncertainty than another poll, or a casino pretending to be a newsroom? The Verge senior reporter Mia Sato is the guest, with trivia and mingling after. Tickets are $25 and include a drink. Phones must be away all night.

Subscribe for the best things to do in NYC.

VINVIVO School of Wine: World of Wine
Scarpetta | 7pm at 355 W 14th St, Meatpacking District

Scarpetta’s VINVIVO wine school is doing a “World of Wine” session, led by their SVP of Brand Operations and resident wine aficionado Alessio de Sensi. You get an interactive overview of winemaking history, proper wine verbiage, and tasting technique, plus four wines with charcuterie and cheese, followed by a pasta course and dessert. Tickets are $160 but that’s pretty similar to what you would have paid at Scarpetta for dinner anyway.

The Banned Wagon
Brooklyn Public Library | 2-6pm at 340 Bushwick Avenue, Bushwick

Penguin Random House's Banned Wagon is a painted truck touring the five boroughs for Banned Books Week, stocked with more than 50 banned and challenged books, from picture books to adult novels. They’re even handing out free copies while supplies last. Scan the QR code on the wagon and a book gets donated to a community in need through First Book, or send a note to your reps through EveryLibrary. It parks at the Bushwick Library branch Monday from 2 to 6pm. Free books and a small act of defiance. Check out all their stops.

Tuesday October 6

⭐ Machine Learning
Manhattan Neighborhood Network | Oct 6-30 at 509 W 38th St, Hell's Kitchen

Machine Learning is the world premiere of a dark comedy by Australian playwright Kate Vozella, in her Off-Broadway debut. Two couples join a research program at a remote facility to help train humanoid companions in human intimacy, and end up reckoning with their own patterns, secrets, and vulnerabilities instead. The cast is stacked with TV faces: Delaney Rowe (also debuting), Michele Selene Ang (13 Reasons Why), Douglas Smith (Big Little Lies), and Emma Ramos (New Amsterdam), directed by Colm Summers. It’s interesting that a play about teaching robots intimacy will probably make you examine your own. I’m checking it out next week and will report back. I have to say I have high expectations for this limited engagement. Tickets start at $43.

Trading Beauty: Art Market Histories
Rizzoli Bookstore | 6pm at 1133 Broadway, NoMad

Valentina Castellani comes to Rizzoli to talk art markets with art advisor Tobias Meyer. She’s celebrating her new book Trading Beauty, an illustrated history of how art gets bought and sold, from medieval altarpieces to today's auction rooms. Castellani peppers the story with the personalities and moments that built the market as we know it, then signs copies after the talk. RSVP for free.

⭐ After Hours: Wanderlust
MoMA | 7-10pm at 11 W 53rd St, Midtown

MoMA's After Hours series returns Tuesday with Wanderlust, an evening built around longing for elsewhere, memory, and escape. Artist-led programming includes a performance by L'Rain, a DJ set from Alexis De La Rosa with dancer Lysis, a TUMBAO-presented performance by Camila Arroyo and Ricardo Daniel, and a participatory workshop with Cassandra Mayela Allen. Five exhibitions stay open all evening, including Nilima Sheikh: Fractured Skies, plus a pop-up bar in the lobby and Sculpture Garden. I love a museum after dark night. Tickets are $30.

Wednesday October 7

On Cloud Wine x The Red Hook Winery: Tour & Tasting
Red Hook Barrel Yard | 6:30pm at 185 Van Dyke St, Red Hook

On Cloud Wine is taking over The Red Hook Winery for an evening tour and tasting led by the winery's owner, Mark Snyder. The night starts in the barrel room then settles into a guided tasting of three wines with light bites. All of it on the Red Hook waterfront with Statue of Liberty views and, if you are lucky, a proper sunset. Tickets are $60.

Icons of Culture: Esperanza Spalding
Perelman Performing Arts Center | 7pm at 251 Fulton St, Fidi

PAC NYC's Icons of Culture series welcomes five-time Grammy winner Esperanza Spalding. The bassist, vocalist, composer, and bandleader sits for a candid conversation about her inspirations and jazz's role in her career, from the Best New Artist Grammy to founding Prismid, her eco-cultural nonprofit hub. She’ll touch on artistic innovation, community wellness, and social justice. The night ends with a special performance of songs. Tickets start at $59.

Thursday October 8

⭐ PaleyFest NY 2026
The Paley Museum | Oct 8-14 at 25 W 52nd St, Midtown

PaleyFest NY takes over the Paley Museum October 8 through 14 with advance screenings and the casts to match. For the uninitiated, it is the TV world's annual fan festival, run by the Paley Center for Media, where networks premiere new seasons with the stars in the room answering questions. The week runs from American Horror Story (Jessica Lange and Sarah Paulson in person) through Dexter's 20th anniversary (Michael C. Hall, Uma Thurman), Tulsa King (Stallone himself), Billy Crystal interviewed by Whoopi Goldberg, and new seasons of The Gilded Age and The Diplomat. Check out the full lineup, tickets range in prices.

Book Crush: Singles Social
Liz's Book Bar | 7:30pm at 315 Smith St, Carroll Gardens

This one’s for the men: Book Crush is a hosted singles night at Liz's Book Bar, run by the dating outfit Asaya. You fill out a 90-second profile beforehand, get 4-6 six-minute introductions with conversation starters provided, and then the night loosens into a party where you mingle, trade numbers, or privately tell the hosts who you would like to see again. The women’s tickets are sold out but there’s still a few spots for men! Tickets are $30.

Fall Festival at Lakeside
LeFrak Center at Lakeside | Oct 8-Nov 1 in Prospect Park

The LeFrak Center at Lakeside is spending all of October as a fall festival. There will be a pumpkin patch, corn maze, carnival games, lawn games, tarot readers, and seasonal snacks and drinks. The headline act is the Haunted Hotel, a 25-minute immersive zombie hotel takeover recommended for ages 13 and up. Entry to the grounds and pumpkin patch is free. I kind of always thought you had to go upstate for something like this. Tickets are $1 per activity ticket, with a $35 all-access pass.

Friday October 9

Noihsaf Bazaar Launch Party
Noihsaf Bazaar | 5-8pm at 135 Wythe St, Williamsburg

Noihsaf Bazaar (fashion spelled backwards), the curated resale marketplace founded by stylist Kate Lindello, is celebrating its first NYC weekend pop-up. The racks will have secondhand Babaà, Dôen, Cordera, and Eckhaus Latta alongside premium vintage and accessories, plus capsule collections from Samet and Scarf Shop, handmade mobiles by artist Peter Witrak, and event-only merch. RSVP for free.

Locating Girlhood: Place and Identity in Early American "Schoolgirl" Art
American Folk Art Museum | 2 Lincoln Square, Upper West Side

The American Folk Art Museum opens Locating Girlhood on October 9, a landmark show of eighteenth- and nineteenth-century needlework and ornamental art made by girls and young women. Nearly a hundred works, many rarely shown because of their fragility, trace how young makers depicted place (pastoral landscapes, gardens, cityscapes, maps) long before American landscape painting got the credit, with works by Black and Native American students expanding the canon. Highlights include a monumental 1747-50 Boston "Fishing Lady" needlework picture and Mary King's 1754 Tree of Life. Admission to the museum is always free, check out full exhibition details.

Saturday October 10

Corn Social
Kitsby Studio | 4pm at 393 Broadway, SoHo

Kitsby Studio is sending corn season off properly with a corn potluck. A long table where everyone brings a dish starring the season's star ingredient. It can be homemade or store-bought, savory or sweet. Everyone brings a plate, everyone gets a seat, and nobody leaves a stranger. Very community forward and I’m into it. Tickets are $25.

Screening: Earth (1930)
Metrograph | 6:30pm at 7 Ludlow St, Lower East Side

Dovzhenko’s final silent feature, a 1930 Ukrainian landmark about the clash between landowning peasants and the modernizers bringing the first tractor to the countryside, screens in 35mm on Saturday. The film has fueled nearly a century of debate over whether it’s Soviet propaganda or a secret celebration of Ukrainian folk culture. There will be a live accompaniment from Fima Chupakhin on piano and synths and Julian Kytasty on bandura and vocals, part of Metrograph’s Dovzhenko: Earth and Empire series. Tickets are $25.

UPRISING/DOWNFALL: Repression and Resistance in the Making of Democracy
Brooklyn Public Library | 7-11pm at 10 Grand Army Plaza, Prospect Heights

The BPL is hosting a late-night teach-in on political resilience and hope. There will be conversations, readings, and debates looking back on America's major democratic movements and the continuous struggle for equity. The night opens at 7pm with a live set from DJ Kofta, then a keynote from physicist Karmela Padavic-Callaghan and Living Colour guitarist Vernon Reid, plus a speaker roster that includes Ava Chin, Dawn Porter, Dr. Uché Blackstock, and Linda Villarosa. Music, performances, and refreshments, guest curated by Brian Tate. Register for free.

Cameras and Coffee: Hahnemühle's Printing Showcase
International Center of Photography | 11am-1pm at 84 Ludlow St, Lower East Side

ICP's monthly meet-up for photographers, collectors, and camera enthusiasts returns Saturday with a printing demo from Hahnemühle, the legacy fine-art paper company, presented with LES camera store K&M. Stop by K&M at 54 Orchard Street between 10:15 and 11am to grab a free Hahnemühle paper samples pack, then head to ICP for the session. Coffee and pastries for purchase. RSVP for free.

Sunday October 11

⭐ Fungus Festival 2026
The Battery | 11am-4pm at The Battery, Financial District

When I last included a mushroom-related event, it became my most engaged with event ever. I think everything I include is cool, but you guys really like mushrooms so I had to include this one too. The New York Mycological Society's fourth annual Fungus Festival takes over The Battery on Sunday. The program includes talks and workshops on everything from eDNA soil sampling and fungal dyes to edible-versus-poisonous mushrooms and the hunt for glowing fungi, plus a mushroom ID station (bring your finds), mushroom food and tinctures, vendors, and a fungi fashion parade where you dress as a mushroom. Basically the most New York festival you’ve never heard of. Totally free, check out the full schedule.

Sushi Con 2026
Pier 36 | 11am-5pm at 299 South St, Lower East Side

The country's largest sushi expo takes over Pier 36 on Sunday with more than 60 exhibitors from Japan, the US, and beyond, and your ticket gets you unlimited tastings of bluefin tuna, uni, caviar, scallops, salmon, A5 Wagyu, and more. The main event is a live 400+ pound bluefin tuna cutting show, with expert chefs carving the fish in front of you and serving the otoro, chutoro, and akami on the spot. Acclaimed restaurants will also be serving premium dishes for purchase. Half-day passes are $135.

What I did last week.

Places or shows I went to over the last week. These are personal recommendations. If I had a cool week, they’ll be cool. If I didn’t, they won’t.

  1. 141 Atelier - Walked into this tiny downtown jewelry store after dim sum. It sits on that stretch of Elizabeth Street just above Canal where the good shops are all inconspicuous and down a flight of steps that’s easy to miss. It’s also right next door to PARK at KIM’s and its very good coffee. Everything is thin and dainty. I almost bought something as a gift for a friend but knew I’d end up keeping it so had the self control to leave.

  2. Deluxe Green Bo - My friend and I left the Mid-Autumn Festival still hungry, so we followed her saved list to this Bayard Street spot for dim sum. Neither of us had been. It was the perfect afternoon snack, and they had us in and out in fifteen minutes.

  3. Threes Brewing - Went to the Gowanus backyard for their Grill & Chill with Lobster Place. The lobster rolls were delicious and for a minute it really still felt like summer. That backyard remains one of my favorite places to sit outside in Brooklyn. They always have fun pop ups too.

  4. Anew Cafe - The cutest little West Village cafe. The design was thoughtful and colorful, pastries were yummy, and the outdoor seating was plentiful despite it being a sunny Saturday morning.

  5. Mazi - Picked up dinner here on my way home. Their greek salad was extremely fresh. It’s kind of impossible to find a good one under $25 these days and theirs was. I think it will become a new weekly staple for me.

  6. Lusardi’s - Spent Friday night at this old-school white-tablecloth Italian spot on the Upper East Side. I mostly go to those new restaurants with wooden tables where everyone shares everything, so it was a nice change to be the youngest table by about fifteen years while everyone around us drank martinis.

If you you’re hosting an event you think is a good fit for City Happenings or if you want to sponsor the newsletter, submit requests here.

Legend for new readers

  • ⭐ = events I am particularly excited about

  • everything else = things I am still really excited about

item.title: Open House New York: The Doors I'm Trying to Get Through
item.description: Still no arch, but there's a midnight pipe-listening session
item.dc:creator: Alexa Weiser
item.content:encoded:
I've been telling people for years that my dream Open House New York moment is climbing the arch at Grand Army Plaza in Brooklyn. I even said it in an interview this summer, like it was a foregone conclusion I'd get there eventually. I went looking for it on the newly announced 2026 lineup and it's nowhere to be found. So that dream is on hold. At least for now.

For anyone not familiar, Open House New York Weekend is three days (October 16-18 this year) where 300+ sites across the five boroughs let you in for tours, talks, and generally just access you can’t normally get. A lot of it is genuinely strange (you can literally tour sewage facilities). That said, I will never stop being fascinated by how the city actually works underneath the parts we see. The subway system, the water towers, the pipes under the street, and the maintenance teams keeping all of it running. I know I’m not alone in this, because the tours into that stuff are always the first to disappear. Ticketed sites go live October 2nd at noon, and if past years are any indication, the good ones go in minutes. A lot of the festival is also just drop-in making it easy for you to pick a neighborhood and just wander into places.

Subscribe now

I’m not going to pretend I have a fully mapped-out route this year, mostly because I’ve gotten my hopes up about tickets I couldn’t actually secure before. Sharing my favorite picks publicly also doesn’t help my odds, but alas, here’s what I’m most excited about.

The Shortlist

If there’s a theme to my list this year, it’s that I seem to be drawn to how things get made. The timing on my first pick is a little uncanny.

The one I’d be most upset to lose is the MTA Arts & Design tour of “In Service” by Christopher Payne (Grand Central Madison, the Dining Concourse, and 42 St-Bryant Park, Saturday, 10-11:30am or 12-1:30pm, ticketed). If you’ve been reading my weekly roundups since September, you might remember me writing about Payne’s industrial photography show at Cooper Hewitt. It made me realize how much manual labor goes into things I’d always assumed were machine-made. This year he's doing an MTA takeover, personally walking small groups through three transit sites and explaining how he actually gets access to photograph a system most of us just rush through. I'm not yet emotionally prepared for the possibility that I won't get in.

Right behind it is finally getting to do the water tower tour I’ve been curious about for a while now (Chelsea, Saturday and Sunday, various times, ticketed). They're one of the most recognizable parts of the New York skyline and also one of the least understood. At least I’m telling myself that so I don’t feel uneducated. I've walked past thousands of them without knowing how they actually work or why every building seems to need one. This tour aims to explain just that.

Then there’s the one that requires real commitment: Midnight Leak Detection with NYC DEP (Civic Center, Friday, midnight or 1am, ticketed). The DEP's Leak Detection team goes out at night, when the city's quiet enough to isolate the very specific sound of pressurized water escaping through a crack. They use equipment that's essentially a giant stethoscope for the street. Apparently they can tell the difference between an actual leak and ordinary water just moving through a pipe. I would like them to come to my apartment this winter and confirm my radiator is, in fact, just absurdly loud and not leaking.

Back to the “watch something get made” theme, I’m hoping to squeeze in Tom’s Sons International Pleating (Garment District, Saturday, 10am-2pm, drop-in), a family-run pleating workshop that’s been open since 1931 and still does work for names like Oscar de la Renta and Vera Wang. I don’t know if they’ve ever touched anything for Issey Miyake, but pleating as a craft immediately sends my brain to a vintage Miyake-adjacent piece I still think about. Either way, watching a 125-year-old family business make garments in real time is right up my alley.

Colossal Media Paint Shop (East Williamsburg, Friday, 10-11am, ticketed) is also on my list. They’re the company behind essentially every hand-painted mural ad you’ve ever seen on the side of a building. Before digital billboards, “walldogs” scaled buildings to paint advertisements entirely by hand, and Colossal is one of the last places keeping that alive. Wear shoes you don’t care about. Wet paint is involved.

And because I have genuine affection for it, I have to include the Gowanus Dredgers Self-Guided Canoe Trips (Gowanus, Saturday and Sunday, 10am-6pm, drop-in). I said (and still believe) that one of New York’s greatest accomplishments is convincing people to voluntarily spend time in the Gowanus Canal. I do respect it though. There's something genuinely lovely about a neighborhood group building their own dock and revitalizing the area. Let me know if any of you actually do this. I might join you.

Finally, NYC Health’s Rat Academy and Rat Walk (Harlem, Friday, ticketed) takes you to a genuine classroom session on rat biology followed by a walk through East Harlem to spot rat conditions in the wild. It doesn’t get more New York than that.

If there’s anyone I can talk to about getting the arch at Grand Army Plaza back onto the lineup, let me know. Until then, tell me what I missed. Scrolling through 300+ listings at 11pm was not an easy feat.

item.title: Things to Do in NYC This Week (Sept 28 - Oct 4)
item.description: Japanese City Pop, sake tastings, and Park Slope’s giant stoop sale
item.dc:creator: Alexa Weiser
item.content:encoded:
On Friday night, I was headed to a show at City Winery and decided to walk a few blocks along the West Side Highway on the way. Somewhere around Pier 57, I looked up and saw one of the most beautiful sunsets I’ve seen in New York City. I walked all the way out to the end of the pier and stood there staring at it long enough that I almost made myself late for the show.

I was completely on my own, but not really. The pier was full of people experiencing the same sunset in their own way. Couples had stopped walking, runners had paused mid-run, and plenty of other people were standing there alone too, all facing the same direction. It felt very communal even though none of us said anything to each other. Some of my best moments in the city are like that. I’m technically around strangers, but I know we’re all sharing the same experience. Even when it’s something annoying, like an announcement confirming our already long subway stop is nowhere close to over, there’s something I love about the collective groan.

Then Saturday I was promised a stormy nor’easter, so I made basically no plans. At least in Prospect Heights, this turned out to be more of a light rain. My husband and his friends have been joking for months about wanting to go to Fogo de Chão, and one friend decided his rainy Saturday birthday was finally the occasion. So at the last minute, we went and ate endless steak. For brunch.

I felt slightly ill for the rest of the weekend, but I have to admit it was fun. Two very different communal experiences, now that I think about it.

Monday September 28

⭐ 2026 Storefront Gala
Storefront for Art & Architecture | 7-10pm at 89 E 42nd St, Midtown

Storefront for Art and Architecture, the nonprofit that has spent more than 40 years exploring how art and architecture shape the places we live, is holding its annual gala inside the Grand Central Oyster Bar. This year honors architecture and design firm SO-IL, arts leader Deana Haggag and artist Mel Chin, with proceeds supporting Storefront’s exhibitions and public programs. Individual gala tickets are kind of out of range, but there’s a much more approachable Gala Party from 10pm-1am, with tickets for $100.

Subscribe for the best things to do in NYC.

Learn to Create Over-the-Top Sundaes
Serendipity3 | 6-8pm at 225 E 60th St, Upper East Side

Serendipity3 is letting you behind the scenes of its famously over-the-top desserts with a hands-on sundae-making class led by chef and creative director Joe Calderone. You’ll brainstorm your dream sundae, then learn how to layer, drizzle, garnish and pair flavors before building your own creation with guidance from Calderone. He’ll also share some of the secrets behind the restaurant’s most iconic sundaes and stories from Serendipity3 along the way. Tickets are $65 and include the two-hour class and all ingredients.

⭐ Japanese City Pop Night
929 Jazz Club | 7pm & 9pm at 56 E 41st St, Midtown

929’s weekly jazz series usually reimagines Asian pop through a jazz lens, and this one-night edition is heading to 1980s Tokyo. J-pop cover band Akari Village will perform jazz-inflected takes on Japanese city pop classics from artists including Tatsuro Yamashita, Mariya Takeuchi and Anri, while also exploring the musical connections between Japanese pop, Canto-pop and Mando-pop during the era. There are two shows at 7pm and 9pm, with a $10 music charge per person. While I’ve never been, I’ve heard great things and the pictures of the space looks especially cozy. Reservations on Resy.

Tuesday September 29

Book Club Salon
Friends From New York | 6-8pm at 126 Crosby St, Soho

For people who like the idea of a book club more than necessarily reading the book, Friends From New York and Housing Works host a monthly salon that’s part author conversation, part hang. This month, Hallie Elizabeth Newton will discuss her debut novel Agnes Lives!, about a fading NYC socialite searching for someone to kill her before her next SoulCycle class, with FFNY founder Heidi Hartwig. There will also be books and signings, plus happy hour from 5-8pm. RSVP for free.

Amigas Means Friends Book Swap
Saturn Road | 6-7:30pm at 276 Court St, Cobble Hill

Amigas Means Friends, a community focused on helping women make new friends, is hosting its first NYC book swap. Bring one or two books you’re ready to part with, then trade them for something new while meeting other women through guided introductions and book-themed conversation prompts. Coming alone is encouraged, and the whole thing is structured to avoid the awkward networking part of meeting strangers. RSVP for free.

Wednesday September 30

Cigars & Comedy
The Stand | 7pm at 116 E 16th St, Union Square

The Stand is pairing its comedy show with a prix-fixe dinner from Sam Braverman, head chef at Lori Jayne. The night starts at 7pm with comedians and guests dining together on dishes including Cuba Frita croquetas, Buffalo 2.0 gnocchi and steak fries with miso chimichurri, before moving into a 9pm show featuring Aaron Berg, Dan Soder, Joe List, Mark Normand, Pete Lee, Ian Lara, Mike Figs and more. Dinner tickets are $98 and include two cigars from Foundation Cigars and a specialty Four Roses cocktail. Show-only tickets start at $43.

Acid Anniversary Party
Farm.One | 7-10pm at 625 Bergen St, Prospect Heights

Farm.One is celebrating the fourth birthday of Acid, its line of fermented hot sauces made with peppers and herbs grown at the indoor farm. For the party, they’re bringing back Pepper Acid for the fall and serving a special cocktail menu featuring Acid, plus pizza from Pizza Party topped with a new hot sauce made from the leftover pepper mash used to produce it. There will also be limited-edition merch, drinks and plenty of pizza. RSVP for free.

Thursday October 1

Harlem Quartet
Five Boroughs Music Festival | 6pm at St. Nicholas Ave, Harlem

Five Boroughs Music Festival is kicking off its 20th anniversary season with the Harlem Quartet, part of its longtime mission to bring chamber music beyond the city’s traditional concert halls and into communities across all five boroughs. The Grammy-winning quartet will make its festival debut with a program spanning Beethoven, Wynton Marsalis, William Grant Still, William Bolcom and others. It’s the first concert in a season that will eventually bring performances to every borough. RSVP for free. Almost all of the upcoming programming is free!

Sake Day 2026
Bin Bin Sake | 5-8pm at 29 Norman Ave, Greenpoint

Bin Bin Sake is celebrating World Sake Day with unlimited tastings of more than 25 sakes selected by its team and distributors. Your ticket gets you a tasting cup to use throughout the night, plus a discount on any bottles you discover and want to bring home. There will also be a market of local art and Japanese crafts, food vendors and a DJ, with the celebration spilling into neighboring Rule of Thirds. Tickets are $18.

⭐ Fall Craft Social
No Booze Babes | 6-9pm at 200 Banker St, Greenpoint

No Booze Babes, a community for sober and sober-curious women and anyone who likes socializing without alcohol, is hosting a cozy fall craft night at Soft Bar. You’ll bedazzle mini pumpkins while a nostalgic movie plays in the background, with plenty of time to meet other people over soft cocktails and other nonalcoholic drinks. Tickets are $35 and include a mini pumpkin, all the decorating supplies and sweet treats.

Friday October 2

Book Magic Live
Rise Literary | All day at 222 W 23rd St, Chelsea

For anyone sitting on a book idea and wondering how it actually becomes a book, Rise Literary is hosting a one-day writers’ retreat inside the Chelsea Hotel. The day is designed to demystify the path from emerging writer to published author, covering everything from building your byline to finding and growing a community around your work. There will be live Q&As with book editors, writing coaches, published authors, and magazine editors with a focus on the practical side of navigating publishing. Tickets are $125.

Explorer Salon: Ghost Stories at The Met
Lit Society x The Met | 5-7pm at 1000 Fifth Ave, Upper East Side

Lit Society by Bond & Grace hosts “Explorer Salons,” small-group cultural outings that use literature as a way into art and history. For this edition, they’re teaming up with Fable & Lark for a guided tour of The Met through the lens of ghost stories, moving from ancient Egyptian funerary traditions to haunted landscapes and unsettling portraits while exploring fear, folklore, death and the supernatural across cultures. You’ll also get curated reading materials beforehand, plus a Lit Society keepsake and a few literary surprises. Tickets are $75.

⭐ Mid-Autumn Festival
Welcome to Chinatown | Friday-Sunday from 1-7pm at 1 Rose St, Chinatown

Welcome to Chinatown and Gotham Park are teaming up for a free, three-day Mid-Autumn Festival beneath the Brooklyn Bridge, with a market highlighting local Asian food businesses, artists and makers. Vendors range from Anna Ye Tea, Homecoming Matcha and Nine Treasures Creamery to ceramics, prints, candles and other goods. Saturday has the biggest cultural program, with family mahjong lessons, mooncake Play-Doh, lantern-making and a lantern parade at 5pm. RSVP for free.

Saturday October 3

NYC Coffee Festival
NYC Coffee Festival | 9am-4:30pm at 100 Dobbin St, Williamsburg

The inaugural NYC Coffee Festival is bringing together specialty roasters for a full day devoted to trying a lot of coffee. Your ticket includes unlimited tastings from participating coffee vendors, with teas and other non-coffee drinks in the mix too, plus live music throughout the day and food available to buy. The festival is split into a morning and afternoon session, with early admission at 9am for anyone who wants an extra hour before the first general admission session starts. There are also limited all-day passes if one coffee session just isn’t enough. Tickets start at $31.

⭐ Super Stoop 2026
Park Slope Civic Council | 11am-4pm throughout Park Slope

Park Slope is turning itself into one giant stoop sale for the second annual Super Stoop. Neighbors across the neighborhood will set up mini pop-up shops and giveaways on their stoops, selling everything from clothing and books to plants, sports equipment and food. There’s no single location, so the idea is to use the event map to wander between participating stoops, browse what your neighbors are getting rid of and see where you end up. They will be publishing a full map so you can plan your stops.

Madison Avenue Fall Gallery Walk
Madison Ave Bid | 10am-5pm from E 57th to E 86th St, Upper East Side

Madison Avenue’s annual fall gallery walk turns a long stretch of the Upper East Side into a free, self-guided art crawl, with dozens of galleries opening their doors for exhibitions plus artist and curator talks throughout the day. This year you can see everything from Baldwin Lee’s 1970s New York photography and contemporary Japanese ceramics to rare Cartier objects and a private Basquiat installation. Sotheby’s is also hosting an Open House with tours and conversations across art, design and luxury. The walk itself is free; talks and some special programs require advance registration. Check out the full list of participating galleries.

⭐ Love Your Library Day
Brooklyn Public Library | All day at branches across Brooklyn

Brooklyn Public Library is turning an ordinary library day into a borough-wide celebration of all the things you can do there beyond checking out books. Branches across Brooklyn will host free concerts, book giveaways, storytimes, crafts, reading groups and workshops throughout the day. Central Library has a plant swap, Silent Book Club and a pickling and fermentation workshop; Park Slope has two family concerts; Dyker has multilingual programming and hands-on science aboard the BioBus; and Sunset Park has gardening and printmaking. Everything is free. Check out the full line up.

Grilled Branzino on Little Island
Piscator x Little Island | All evening at Pier 55, Hudson River Park

Piscator, the whole-branzino pop-up that has a habit of selling out almost immediately, is closing out its New York season with a dinner on Little Island before heading to LA for the winter. The concept centers around whole branzino grilled over an open flame and served outdoors, and this time you’ll be eating it on Little Island. Tickets drop in about an hour. Move quickly. Maybe you’ll even catch a sunset like last Friday’s.

Sunday October 4

Spellbound Fall Market
Pleased to Meet You | 11am-6pm at 93 Scott Ave, Bushwick

Pleased to Meet You is kicking off spooky season with a free fall market at Honey’s, bringing together small businesses selling vintage clothing, jewelry, accessories, homewares, candles and more. Beyond shopping, there will be live music, astrological readings and tooth gems, plus drinks and food available to buy from Honey’s and other vendors. You can also head up to the rooftop for views while you take a break from browsing. RSVP for free.

Blanc de Noir Wine Class
Place des Fêtes | 1-3pm at 212 Greene Ave, Clinton Hill

Place des Fêtes is hosting a wine class devoted to blanc de noirs, white wines made using red-skinned grapes. Sommelier Jessica Lee will lead a tasting of five wines, one sparkling and four still, while explaining how they’re made, what red grapes can bring to a wine without extended skin contact and why more winemakers are experimenting with the style. Tickets are $100 and include all wines and seasonal snacks.

What I did last week.

Places or shows I went to over the last week. These are personal recommendations. If I had a cool week, they’ll be cool. If I didn’t, they won’t.

  1. Francesco - Simple Italian food with pastries that will change your life. A friend took me for brunch during prime time and there was also no line. On a weekend in Soho. Let that sink in.

  2. Ask a Fuckboy - I went to a comedy show about…well, fuckboys. At each show, comics present unhinged dating stories and a panel of "fuckboys" weighs in. They pop up around NYC every few weeks, and if you have your own dating horror story, you can submit it to be featured. Kind of a great way to get payback.

  3. Apapacho - New fancy Mexican restaurant in Park Slope. You walk into a room with a stylish long bar that would be perfect for an early date before reaching the dining room. The Dobladitas de Camarón were the hit for me.

  4. Sub-Mission - The hidden cocktail lounge beneath Mission Ceviche now has live music Wednesday through Saturday. It’s dark and moody with an intimate feel, the food was great and the pisco sours were both delicious and strong. Unsurprisingly, the ceviche was still the best thing on the menu.

I can’t in good conscience put Fogo de Chao on here even though I thoroughly enjoyed my crazy brunch there.

item.title: Things to Do in NYC This Week (Sept 21 - 27)
item.description: Art fairs take over, your chance to try Semma, and a mushroom walk
item.dc:creator: Alexa Weiser
item.content:encoded:
A small group of friends had plans for a grand Saturday night out. We made the mistake (or maybe not) of first meeting at one of their apartments. It wasn’t long before we decided to order in.

Our grand night out became a grand night in, eating takeout Indian on paper plates on my friend’s living room floor. It couldn’t have been better if we had planned it. In fact, I think planning it would have ruined it. She would have cleared off the dining room table, we would have coordinated what to order in advance, someone would have brought dessert. Basically it would have become a dinner party.

Instead, we just kept sitting around chatting until it became clear we weren’t going anywhere. I spend a lot of this newsletter convincing you (and mostly myself) to leave the house. Getting dressed up to end up staying in is pretty nice too though.

Monday September 21

Narrative Change Summit
SVA Theatre | 9:30am-7pm at 333 W 23rd St, Chelsea

As part of Climate Week, the Climate Film Festival is hosting a full day of talks on how film, TV, journalism, social media and other forms of storytelling can actually get people to engage with climate issues. Sessions range from how reality TV can reach audiences who tune out traditional climate messaging and how NBCUniversal incorporates sustainability into its productions, to using horror and comedy to tell climate stories, making scientific data resonate and reaching sports fans through teams like the Seattle Seahawks. There are also conversations with local leaders, journalists, filmmakers and creators throughout the day, plus a networking hour. You can register for the full summit or drop in for individual sessions. Check out the full agenda.

Subscribe for the best things to do in NYC.

Opera Italiana Is in the Air
Naumburg Bandshell | 6:30-8pm in Central Park

Italian opera takes over Central Park for a free open-air concert celebrating the International Day of Peace. The Opera Italiana Orchestra, which brings together musicians from the Met Opera and New York Philharmonic alongside students from Juilliard and Manhattan School of Music, will perform selections from La Bohème, Turandot, The Barber of Seville, William Tell and Manon Lescaut. The program also includes the world premiere of Everwander by Juilliard Pre-College student Ethan Hsu, performed alongside tenor Alessio Borraggine and soprano Daniela Machado. It’s free and open to everyone.

Tuesday September 22

An UNMUTED x Network 20/20 Debate: Leave the UN?
UNMUTED | 6:30pm in Lower Manhattan (location on RSVP)

UNMUTED and Network 20/20 are hosting a live debate on whether the U.S. should leave the United Nations. Arguing in favor is Taufiq Rahim, a senior fellow at New America with a background in foreign policy, while former U.S. Ambassador to the UN for Management and Reform Chris Lu will argue against. Lu spent three years working on U.S. negotiations over the UN budget and reform, so the conversation should get fairly deep into what the U.S. actually pays for, what it gets in return and whether withholding funding would create leverage or weaken American influence. Rekha Shanmugam will moderate. Tickets are $30.

⭐ NYC in Transit
Film Forum | 6pm at 209 W Houston St, Greenwich Village

For the New York Transit Museum’s 50th anniversary, Film Forum is screening a series of movies where NYC public transit gets a starring role. Tuesday’s program focuses on the city’s elevated trains, led by Stations of the Elevated, Manfred Kirchheimer’s wordless 1981 film capturing graffiti-covered trains moving through the city, set to music by Charles Mingus and Aretha Franklin. It’s paired with three shorts, including D.A. Pennebaker’s Daybreak Express, filmed from a train and edited to Duke Ellington, and Stan Brakhage’s footage of the now-demolished Third Avenue El. Tickets are $18.

Wednesday September 23

Jazz in the Garden
With Others | 5-8pm at 340 Bedford Ave, Williamsburg

With Others is bringing back its Jazz in the Garden series for the final two Wednesdays of September, with live jazz and bottles of wine in its Williamsburg backyard. The music runs from 5-8pm and the best part (for me) is that dogs are welcome. Great way to take advantage of one of the last stretches of warm-weather evenings. A limited number of tables can be reserved on Resy, but most of the patio is being held for walk-ins.

Drink Curiously: Languages of Taste
Bar Heretic | 6-8pm at 270 Clermont Ave, Fort Greene

This introductory class is designed to make the language of wine a little less intimidating. James Sligh of Children’s Atlas of Wine will lead an interactive tasting focused on figuring out what you actually like and how to describe it, with five wines to taste along the way. He puts together detailed maps and tasting sheets to help you visualize the regions. The thought and detail that goes into them is incredible - I’ve always learned something new at his events. Tickets are $65.

Manhatta x Semma
Manhatta | All night at 28 Liberty St, Fidi

If you’ve spent the last few years unsuccessfully trying to get a reservation at Semma, this is your chance to finally try the food. For one night only, Semma chef Vijay Kumar is joining Manhatta executive chef Michele Brogioni for a five-course dinner combining Kumar’s South Indian cooking with Brogioni’s contemporary American menu. A portion of proceeds from each dinner will benefit City Harvest. Tickets are $195.

Thursday September 24

⭐ Art Book Fair
MoMA PS1 | Thursday–Sunday at 22-25 Jackson Ave, Long Island City

Printed Matter’s NY Art Book Fair returns for its 20th anniversary with more than 300 artists, independent publishers and booksellers from around the world taking over MoMA PS1. Beyond browsing an overwhelming amount of art books, zines and other printed matter, there’s a full schedule of book launches and signings, talks, workshops, performances and live music throughout the weekend. This year also includes a Reading Room curated by the African Art Book Fair. Opening night is Thursday from 7-10pm ($60), followed by the regular fair Friday–Sunday ($10). CHeck out tickets and full schedule.

260 Madison Opening Reception
260 Madison | 6-10pm at 260 Madison Ave, Midtown

A vacant Midtown office tower is being temporarily transformed into a massive artist-run exhibition, with more than 50 established and emerging artists taking over a former Duane Reade storefront and an entire 23,000-square-foot office floor. The work spans sculpture, video and new media, with artists using the building’s architecture and remnants of its former life to explore surveillance, AI, control and the systems shaping how we work and live. The exhibition only runs for two months, but Thursday is the opening reception and a chance to explore the spaces at night. It’s free to attend.

Also, basically every art fair begins and every museum opens a show. Some that I’m looking forward to:

  • Independent 20th Century is focused on broadening our understanding of 20th century art and featuring recognized artists alongside lesser known voices. Held at the the Breuer building.

  • The Armory Show is the biggest of the fairs and brings the world’s leading international contemporary and modern art galleries to the Javits Center.

  • Clio Art Fair targets artists without any gallery representation, meaning they are free to deviate from accepted practices.

  • The New Museum kicks off its new season with a full turnover of new exhibitions, the biggest highlight being Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony which will feature Jafa’s most celebrated works over his 40 year career.

Friday September 25

⭐ Downtown Gallery Night: After Hours
Downtown Gallery Night | 6-8pm at galleries across Downtown Manhattan

More than 80 downtown galleries and art spaces are staying open late for one night for Armory Week. You can use the Showrunner app to see all participating galleries and map out a route, and the night continues with drinks at YveYANG Gallery until 9pm.

icchā
BMCC Tribeca Performing Arts Center | Friday & Saturday at 7:30pm at 199 Chambers St, Tribeca

Kathak artist and choreographer Barkha Patel performs a 60-minute solo work exploring the idea that unfulfilled desires can be carried through generations. In icchā, Patel is visited in a dream by her maternal ancestors, who ask her to express the desires they were unable to fulfill during their own lives, touching on survival, loss, intimacy and the denial of dance and self-expression. The performance combines kathak and garba with original music and set design, using dance to explore what we inherit from the women who came before us. Tickets are $40.

⭐ New York Film Festival
Film at Lincoln Center | Sept 25 - Oct 12 at Lincoln Center & venues across NYC

The New York Film Festival returns for its 64th edition with films from established directors and emerging filmmakers from around the world. This year’s Main Slate includes 34 films from 31 countries, alongside Spotlight screenings, restored classics and other programs. Opening night is James Gray’s Paper Tiger, a New York thriller starring Adam Driver, Miles Teller and Scarlett Johansson, while other major premieres include new films from Tony Gilroy, Luca Guadagnino and Ava DuVernay. Most screenings are at Lincoln Center, with additional screenings at BAM, Museum of the Moving Image, and venues in the Bronx and Staten Island. Check out the full line up.

Saturday September 26

Run & Recover
Brasil Run Club | 11am at 3 Freeman Alley, Lower East Side

Run & Recover returns for a special Brazilian Independência Month edition, starting with an 11am community run through the city accompanied by a DJ bike. At noon, everyone heads back to UNTITLED for a Run & Recover Party combining fitness, recovery and wellness activities with music. You can join for the run, the party, or make a full afternoon of it. I’m not usually one to push a run club, but theirs look genuinely fun. If you don’t believe me, watch this first. Tickets are $20.

Joan’s Friends Screening & Conversation
Independent 20th Century | 1pm at 548 W 22nd St, Chelsea

As part of Independent 20th Century, a screening of the 2015 documentary Joan’s Friends will offer a more personal look at artist Joan Mitchell through the people who knew her. After the film, its creator Guy Bloch-Champfort joins poet and critic John Yau for a conversation about Mitchell and her work, moderated by Sotheby’s Alya Sama. Bloch-Champfort will also sign copies of his book Joan Mitchell: By Her Friends, which collects interviews with people from Mitchell’s life. It’s free to attend with fair admission. Fair tickets are $48.

Woven Through Time
Victor Gallery | 6-9pm at 232 E 59th St, Midtown East

Victor Gallery is bringing together rugs from three different perspectives: antique pieces from its own collection, contemporary rugs from Turquoise Mountain and works by artist Ido Michaeli. The evening highlights Central Park Carpets, Michaeli’s collaboration with Afghan weavers through Turquoise Mountain, with a selection of the carpets on view alongside a short talk and open conversation about the project and the relationship between contemporary art and traditional craft. RSVP for free.

Sunday September 27

⭐ Festival Day
Brooklyn Book Festival | 10am-6pm around Brooklyn Borough Hall, Brooklyn Heights

The Brooklyn Book Festival comes to an end with its main Festival Day which brings a full day of free readings and conversations to stages around Borough Hall. There’s a pretty ridiculous lineup of authors including Marlon James, Colson Whitehead, Douglas Stuart, Tracy K. Smith, Tayari Jones, Sigrid Nunez and more. There are dozens of panels running simultaneously across fiction, nonfiction, poetry and comics, covering everything from Toni Morrison and NYC’s underground music scene to food writing, friendship, horror and the secrets hidden in NYC libraries. One of the biggest events closes out the afternoon with Marlon James and Colson Whitehead in conversation about their new novels and the complicated cities at the center of them. Everything is free. Check out the full schedule.

Mushroom Walk
Wild & Curious | 4pm meeting on the Upper West Side

Spend two hours hunting for mushrooms growing wild in Central Park with guides Matthew and Anna, who’ll teach the group how to spot and identify different varieties and explain the role fungi play in the park’s ecosystem. The walk also includes a mushroom tasting and ends with a hands-on art session inspired by what you find, with activities like sketching, sun prints and texture rubbings. No mushroom or art experience required. Tickets are $45.

Atlantic Antic
Atlantic Avenue | 12-6pm from Fourth Ave to Hicks St, South Brooklyn

Brooklyn’s oldest and largest street festival is back for its 51st year, taking over 10 blocks of Atlantic Avenue with hundreds of local businesses and vendors. This year includes more than 80 food vendors and 130 local merchants and craft vendors, plus live music and performances throughout the route. There’s also the returning “Antic Sing” live singing competition, Middle Eastern music and dancing at the Clinton Street stage, and three dedicated kids’ areas with everything from circus performances to pony rides. Check out the full vendor line up.

What I did last week.

Places or shows I went to over the last week. These are personal recommendations. If I had a cool week, they’ll be cool. If I didn’t, they won’t.

  1. Broad Strokes - You only have a few more days to see this hilarious show which closes September 25th. Cat Cohen puts on a performance that is part stand up routine and part Broadway musical. She is impossible to not laugh with. This girl is going places.

  2. Blue Ribbon Sushi Sake - Blue Ribbon Downing Street Bar, which used to occupy this space, was my favorite date night spot back when I lived in the West Village. Maybe it was the nostalgia, but I had to try their new(ish) concept. It’s still as intimate as I remember but now a sushi bar. I shared a sashimi plate with a friend before a show but will be back for the omakase. Everything was fresh and delicious and unlike many omakases in the city, you’re not on the clock for a 60 minute seating.

  3. Mulan - This retelling of the classic story combined classical Chinese dance and martial arts with original music, elaborate costumes and a massive revolving stage. It was fun to see the story of a character I love so much extended and the setting at the David H. Koch Theatre was spectacular, as always. Sadly the NYC run has ended but luckily the ballet season debut is just around the corner.

  4. Fiaschetteria Pistoia - Stopped in for a tiramisu at the end of a night and ended up with a full salad and pasta too. Another one of my longtime favorite spots, both because of the simple yet incredible food and the charming little setting. I’ve tried more times than I can count to rent it out for an event but they stand firm that they don’t do that and I respect it.

  5. Masalawala - I realized how little I eat Indian food despite it being one of my favorite cuisines. This was an easy neighborhood spot to order in from. I’m going to throw it into the rotation.
