item.title: Things to Do in NYC This Week (Sept 14 - 20)
item.description: NYC is showing off this week
item.dc:creator: Alexa Weiser
item.content:encoded:
Friends were visiting from out of town, so despite the pouring rain, I trekked up to the Upper East Side to see them for brunch on Sunday. Between mouthfuls of shakshuka, I looked outside and the miserable day had turned completely sunny. I had a lazy Sunday afternoon planned, but it suddenly felt wrong to just get on the subway and go home.

I remembered that the Christopher Payne exhibit at Cooper Hewitt was closing soon, so I wandered over by myself. It was definitely worth the detour. I’d also never really noticed how peaceful the garden and sitting area out front are. I don’t know if it was nearly empty because it was following the rain or if it’s just a hidden gem. I’ll have to come back with a book to find out.

Afterwards I started wandering down Madison with the vague goal of finding a bridesmaid dress and ended up walking nearly 40 blocks and trying on basically everything except that. That’s when my feet started hurting (I left the house in mini cowboy boots after failing to find my rain boots in a rush to catch the Q) and I finally called it. I came home without a bridesmaid dress but with a running list of brown and burgundy things I now want. Excellent timing considering I just paid an organizer to help me on my journey to own fewer clothes.

Anyway, NYC is really showing off right now. The hardest part about writing this week’s letter was cutting things. I try to keep each letter to around 20 events so it’s actually a curation of things I would want to go to instead of just a list of everything happening in the city. This week I could have very easily included twice as many.

Monday September 14

⭐ Jewelry Creators: Dynamic Duos and Generational Gems
Rizzoli Bookstore | 6pm at 1133 Broadway, Nomad

For Fashion Week, jewelry historian and author Beth Bernstein is bringing together some of the designers and families featured in her new book, Jewelry Creators, which looks at the partnerships and generational legacies behind 22 jewelry brands. She’ll be joined by Monica Rich Kosann, Corina Madilian of Single Stone, sisters Kim and Nicole Carosella of Sorellina, father-son duo Martin and Mark Klein of Julius Klein, and fifth-generation diamantaire Jade Trau for a conversation, Q&A and book signing. RSVP for free.

Subscribe for the best things to do in NYC.

The Last Bohemians Film Screening
SVA Theatre | 6pm at 333 W 23rd St, Chelsea

Artist Timothy Goodman’s short documentary series profiles eight longtime residents of the Chelsea Hotel, some of whom have lived there for more than 45 years, and the creative lives they’ve built inside one of NYC’s most mythologized buildings. The night starts with drinks, music and live painting, followed by the screening at 7pm and a Q&A with Design Matters host Debbie Millman and several of the residents featured in the film. The program also includes Mon Taxi, a short film selected for this year’s Tribeca Festival. RSVP for free.

Tuesday September 15

Ego Death
L’Apéro by L’Appartement 4F | 6:30pm & 8pm at 115 Montague St, Brooklyn Heights

Ego Death is popping up at L’Appartement 4F’s wine bar for a one-night, eight-course omakase that puts a French-ish, zero-waste spin on the traditional sushi experience. Chef Shom Mazumder, who has worked at Bridges, Estela and The Four Horsemen, is serving bistro and izakaya-inspired small plates, nigiri, bouillabaisse and dessert, with optional wine pairings from L’Apéro’s sommelier. Tickets are $144.

Kimchi Workshop
KinKa | 7pm at 63 E 7th St, East Village

Learn to make your own kimchi at KinKa’s hands-on workshop. The hour-long class covers the basics of fermentation and of making kimchi, with room to experiment with ingredients once you get the technique down. You’ll finish with a tasting of fresh kimchi and tofu and take home a bag of your own kimchi. Tickets are $82.

Wednesday September 16

⭐ Tom Yum Week
Tom Yum | September 16-30 at various Thai restaurants around the city

NYC’s first Tom Yum Week pairs 17 Thai restaurants with 36 artists and creatives, turning meals into installations and interactive experiences inspired by Thai food and culture. Each restaurant is doing something different, from a tom yum sorbet whose ingredients become characters at SkyIce to a digital fortune-telling menu at Sala Thai, a dish translated into sound at Gigi Curry and Noodle Bar, and a film served as part of the meal at Lalyn. The two-week festival is built around the Thai idea of yum, or mixing, bringing together food, art, sound, film and technology in different ways across the city. Check out the full list of participating restaurants and events.

Rhode Island Meets the Riviera
Platform by the James Beard Foundation | 6:30pm at Pier 57, Chelsea

The James Beard Foundation is bringing some of Rhode Island’s most exciting chefs to NYC for a one-night dinner inspired by the French Riviera. James Beard Award semifinalists Robert Andreozzi and William Rietzel will reinterpret New England seafood and Rhode Island classics through a French lens, with a menu including oysters with rosé granita, rock crab fazzoletti, Rhode Island bouillabaisse and tarte tropézienne. The night starts with cocktails and hors d’oeuvres, followed by a multi-course dinner with wine pairings and a Q&A with the chefs. Tickets start at $185.

Thursday September 17

⭐ The Atlantic Festival
The Atlantic | Thursday - Saturday at venues around the city

The Atlantic is bringing its annual festival to NYC for three days of conversations spanning politics, culture, technology, business and media, plus live podcasts, performances, book talks and film screenings. This year’s very stacked speaker list includes Pete Buttigieg, Malcolm Gladwell, Florence Pugh, Padma Lakshmi, Colin Kaepernick, Whitney Wolfe Herd, Senator Mark Kelly, Kara Swisher, Lina Khan, Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan, among many others. Most of the main programming takes place at PAC NYC, but they’re taking parts of the festival out into the city. Check out the full schedule, passes are pricey but there’s some free and lower cost events taking place as well. I’m most excited about Saturday’s free discussion on America’s reading crisis at the Brooklyn Public Library.

Salon Creatives Vol. VII
Casa La Femme | 6:30-9pm at 140 Charles St, West Village

Salon Creatives is an “(un)professional” gathering for NYC’s creative community, bringing together filmmakers, musicians, artists, dancers, writers, photographers and other creative types. The idea is less traditional networking and more meeting potential collaborators and friends, swapping resources and funding opportunities, and getting into conversations with people working on interesting things. There’ll be a guest speech and community toast, but most of the night is left open for mingling. RSVP for free.

⭐ Gimme a Sign!
SoHo Playhouse | 7pm at 15 Vandam St, Soho

Comedian Bailey Swilley brings her solo show Gimme a Sign! to SoHo Playhouse after two acclaimed runs at the Edinburgh Fringe. Part comedy and part ghost story, the show follows Swilley after the unexpected death of her father and her subsequent obsession with looking for signs from the other side. References range from Britney Spears and Blink-182 to a particularly memorable trip to Costco. It runs September 17th and 20th, but tonight’s performance also includes a 6pm pre-show “Crappy Hour,” with drinks and a guided conversation about mortality and the people we’ve lost. Tickets are $37.

Pacific Island Film Festival
PIFF | Thursday-Sunday at various locations in Manhattan

The Pacific Island Film Festival brings four days of films and events celebrating storytelling from across Oceania, with screenings at Playwrights Horizons, the National Museum of the American Indian, Village East by Angelika, and AMC Lincoln Square. Saturday is the biggest day, with seven curated screenings spanning documentaries, features and shorts exploring identity, culture and community, including films from Hawaiʻi, Samoa, Tonga, Aotearoa and beyond. The festival wraps Sunday with a community screening followed by a closing gala featuring awards, a Changemakers Talk with Hawaiʻi writers and actors, and live music. Events are ticketed but some are free. Check out the full lineup.

Friday September 18

⭐ Book Design in the Age of Slop
Microsoft Research Lab x AIGA | 6:30-8:30pm at 300 Lafayette St, Soho

As AI-generated content floods basically every corner of the internet, AIGA is hosting a conversation about why thoughtful, human book design might matter more than ever. Award-winning designers Kevin Barrett Kane and Emma Christine Hall of Benson & Benson will look at how books have survived past technological upheavals, from the printing revolution to the Kindle, and make the case for specialization and analog-informed design in the age of algorithms and automation. Tickets start at $11.

Not-A-Normal Fall Show
One Hanson Place | Sep 18-20 & 25-27 at One Hanson Place, Fort Greene

Not-A-Normal Show returns to One Hanson Place for two weekends of vintage and independent shopping, with more than 150 dealers, designers, artists and makers taking over the landmark former bank. Each weekend has a different lineup spanning vintage and contemporary fashion, jewelry, accessories, furniture, home goods, art, beauty and more, so there’s a reason to go twice. Fridays have early-access shopping followed by an evening with music and drinks, while Saturdays and Sundays are open throughout the day. Tickets start at $28. Despite being over-marketed, this is still one of the best vintage shows in the city. Check out my full vintage guide from earlier this summer if you want something more lowkey.

A Baby For Me? No Thank You, Please!
Soho Playhouse | Friday & Saturday at 15 Vandam St, Soho

Comedian Bailey Swilley’s 50-minute solo show takes on the pressure to have kids after getting married. After family members assume she’ll change her mind about not wanting children, she goes down a rabbit hole of TikTok, self-help books, podcasts and Reddit threads trying to figure out how she actually feels. The result is a comedy about expectations, trusting your own instincts and one particularly enlightening trip to the gynecologist. Tickets are $26.

Saturday September 19

⭐ The Essence of Us: A Cuban Story
92NY | 7pm at 1395 Lexington Ave, Upper East Side

92NY opens its new dance season with an unusual combination of documentary film and live performance centered on contemporary Cuban dance. The night was originally supposed to premiere a new work created by Cuban-born choreographer Pedro Ruiz with Havana’s Malpaso Dance Company, but visa barriers made it impossible for the company to travel to New York. Instead, filmmaker Nel Shelby traveled to Havana and documented Ruiz creating the piece with Malpaso, capturing the dancers, their creative process and what it means to continue making art in contemporary Cuba. The resulting Spanish-language film, The Essence of Us: A Cuban Story, gets its world premiere here, followed by a live performance from Ballet Hispánico. Tickets start at $45.

Erasing Borders Dance Festival
Kaye Playhouse | Saturday & Sunday at 6pm at 695 Park Ave, Upper East Side

The Indo-American Arts Council’s annual Erasing Borders Dance Festival returns for its 18th year, bringing together artists working across Indian classical and contemporary dance. Each night features a different lineup spanning Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kuchipudi, Mohiniyattam, Odissi and more. The program explores stories of devotion drawn from Indian culture and spirituality. Tickets start at $20.

NYC Slice + Pint Crawl Launch Party
Threes Brewing | 6-9pm at 113 Franklin St, Greenpoint

Threes Brewing and Scott’s Pizza Tours are launching In The Fold, a limited-edition pilsner specifically brewed to pair with a New York slice. The launch party includes the first pours paired with pizza, food from Grand Army, and a Vinyl Tap DJ set. It also kicks off a month-long crawl featuring eight pizzerias across the city. With a pizza passport, hit four of the eight stops between September 19 and October 19 and you’re entered for the grand prize. 10% of sales of the beer benefit Slice Out Hunger. RSVP for free to the launch party.

Sunday September 20

⭐ Brooklyn Book Festival
Brooklyn Book Festival | September 20-28 at various Brooklyn venues

One of NYC’s biggest literary events returns for nine days of free and low-cost programming, culminating in its flagship Festival Day around Brooklyn Borough Hall on September 27th. This year’s lineup includes Marlon James, Joyce Carol Oates, Colson Whitehead, Douglas Stuart, Tracy K. Smith and dozens more, with talks and readings across eight indoor and outdoor stages, plus a Literary Marketplace. The week also includes Bookend events at venues across all five boroughs and a dedicated Children’s Day on September 26 with readings, workshops, performances and book signings. See the full schedule & details.

EcoArts Festival
Governors Island | 11am-4pm at Colonels Row, Governors Island

To kick off Climate Week, Artichoke Dance Company’s EcoArts Festival takes over Governors Island with a day of art, dance and hands-on activities centered around the environment. The lineup includes contemporary dance performances, installations exploring NYC waterways and environmental systems, plus workshops in papermaking and textile reuse and even a mock catering performance serving edible bugs. RSVP for free.

⭐ Cheese Omakase
Metro Cheese Club x Frank’s House | 6pm at 133 Clinton Ave, Fort Greene

Posh is teaming up with Metro Cheese Club and Frank’s House for an intimate 12-course cheese omakase with just 25 guests. The dinner is designed to prove that cheese can work with just about anything, moving beyond a traditional cheese tasting with unexpected pairings that range from surf and turf all the way through dessert, plus drinks to match. Basically my dream come true. Request a seat to be one of the lucky few who get to partake.

What I did last week.

Places or shows I went to over the last week. These are personal recommendations. If I had a cool week, they’ll be cool. If I didn’t, they won’t.

  1. Made in America: The Industrial Photography of Christopher Payne - In this exhibit at the Cooper Hewitt, Payne digs into the connection between factory workers and the finished products they create. It was shocking to see how so many small manual processes contribute to the manufacturing of goods we (or I) assumed were machine-made. You have about 2 weeks left to check it out.

  2. Cafe D’Alsace - In a shocking development, my husband made our weekend brunch reservation. I might even let him do it again. Good shakshuka. Perfect for a museum day warm up.

  3. Tanya Taylor - I’m on the hunt for a bridesmaid dress and was drawn into the store on a walk by the flowy, hand-painted dresses in the window. I’d seen the brand before, but had never appreciated how special the pieces are until seeing them in person. I now want basically everything in here.

  4. Buddy’s - I went to Buddy’s for the launch of Jameson’s “America’s Biggest Round”, where they’re putting up an up to $5 million nationwide bar tab for football fans throughout the season. You can scan QR codes at participating bars to claim drink rebates or you can just claim them here if the whole treasure hunt idea isn’t your thing.

item.title: Things to Do in NYC This Week (Sept 8 - 13)
item.description: J Balvin in Soho, a Caribbean literary festival, a Shonda Rhimes deep dive, and more
item.dc:creator: Alexa Weiser
item.content:encoded:
The last month has been one of the most intensely jam-packed periods of my life. I had four back-to-back weddings, all in different parts of the world, on top of work (no, I do not do this letter full time), travel, and trying to maintain some semblance of normal life. I genuinely wanted to do every single thing I committed to over the last month, but my body is now making it very clear that something has to give. I’m extremely excited to now be staying put in NYC for five full weeks, just in time for my favorite stretch of the year.

Fashion Week is starting and I’m about to begin the annual search for my light jackets so I can wear them during the two perfect weeks of the year when they’re actually practical. On the topic of clothes, I actually hired a closet organizer to help me do a full cleanout and to reorganize everything. I’ve toyed with the idea of doing this for years but I’ve avoided it because I’m too attached to my clothes to get rid of anything. I’m hoping an objective third party (aka not my husband) will make this process easier. Realistically I’ll probably end up keeping everything and just finding more creative ways to organize in my limited closet space.

Tuesday September 8

⭐ Alison Nguyen: Prior Occupants
The High Line | 7-8:30pm at 14th St & 10th Ave, Chelsea

High Line Art is premiering Prior Occupants, a new film by artist Alison Nguyen exploring the little-known nuclear history of Westbeth, the former Bell Laboratories complex that was involved in research connected to the atomic bomb. The film was commissioned with the CHANEL Culture Fund, a global arts program that partners with cultural institutions to fund new work, elevate overlooked stories, and support experimentation. After the screening, Nguyen will discuss the film and how old buildings like Westbeth and the High Line can preserve, or erase, pieces of their histories with High Line Art curator Taylor Zakarin. RSVP for free.

Subscribe for the best things to do in NYC.

RISK! Live Show & Story Slam
Caveat | 7pm at 21 A Clinton St, Lower East Side

The long-running storytelling podcast RISK! comes to Caveat for a live show built around true stories that haven’t been heard on the podcast before. Three featured storytellers, including comedian Liza Treyger, will tell stories around the night’s theme, “That’s a Surprise”, followed by three audience volunteers who’ll get the chance to tell short stories of their own. The stories can range from funny to heartbreaking, and ones recorded at the show may later make it onto the podcast. Tickets are $18.

Wednesday September 9

⭐ Brooklyn Caribbean Literary Festival
Various hosts | Sep 9-13 at various Brooklyn locations

The Brooklyn Caribbean Literary Festival returns for five days of conversations, readings, screenings and food programming celebrating Caribbean and diasporic storytelling. This year’s theme, “One Hand Don’t Clap”, focuses on migration, collective survival and the ways storytelling can preserve memory and reimagine belonging. The lineup is stacked, with Marlon James, Edwidge Danticat, Sister Nancy, Julia Alvarez, Imani Perry and Nicole Dennis-Benn, plus conversations on everything from Caribbean food and publishing to Jamaica’s coastline and the experience of “barrel children.” Check out the full schedule of events. Some are free and others require tickets.

Summer Seafood Clam Bake
The Clam | Wednesdays & Thursdays through September at 420 Hudson St, West Village

The Clam is doing an old-school seafood feast every Wednesday and Thursday through the end of summer, centered around a big clam bake with Maine lobster, blue claw crabs, Gulf shrimp, top neck clams, corn, potatoes and green beans with lemon-garlic butter. Lunch is $65 for two courses, while dinner is $95 and adds dessert. Tickets on Resy.

Thursday September 10

Jennifer Gersten: Solo Concert
Scandinavia House | 7:30pm at 58 Park Ave, Murray Hill

Violinist Jennifer Gersten performs a program of experimental contemporary music by composers based in Scandinavia, with three works being performed in the US for the first time. The six solo violin pieces explore some pretty unusual sounds, inspired by everything from bird calls and fragmented speech to butterfly wings. The concert ends with the world premiere of a new piece Gersten created with Norwegian composer and bassist Inga Margrete Aas. Tickets are $20.

David Duchovny: About Time
The Great Hall at Cooper Union | 7pm at 7 E 7th St, East Village

David Duchovny joins actress and author Gina Gershon for a conversation tied to his new poetry collection, About Time. They’ll talk about Duchovny’s unusually varied career across acting, novels, filmmaking and music, and how his creative work has approached subjects like grief, aging, failure and mortality. The conversation will also explore what it means to keep creating outside the field you’re best known for. Duchovny will sign copies of About Time after the event. Tickets start at $20.

NY Fashion Week Party at Original Story
Original Story | 7-10pm at 86 Dobbin St, Greenpoint

Original Story is hosting a Fashion Week party centered around discovering emerging designers and their upcoming collections. You’ll be able to meet the people behind the brands and shop pieces before the new season, with live jazz from the Dylan Kries Trio, a complimentary Desolas Mezcal cocktail bar and a live photo booth throughout the night. Cocktail attire is encouraged. Tickets are $68.

Friday September 11

⭐ J Balvin x Vélez Fashion Week Pop-Up
Shopify NY | Sep 11-13 from 11am-6pm at 131 Greene St, Soho

J Balvin and Colombian fashion brand Vélez are taking over Shopify’s Soho space for a three-day Fashion Week pop-up celebrating Latin fashion, craft, music and culture. The “Artisan Gang in the City” experience will showcase the J Balvin x Vélez collaboration alongside new and upcoming work from the brand, bringing Colombian craftsmanship to NYC for the weekend. Free to visit, you can browse the collection in advance.

New York City Global Food & Culture Festival
Bryant Park | Sep 11-13 from 10am-7pm in Bryant Park

Bryant Park hosts a three-day outdoor festival bringing together food and vendors from around the world. There’ll be food trucks and international street food, alongside a market of clothing, handmade goods, beauty products and other specialty items. The weekend will also have live music and cultural performances throughout the park. RSVP for free. You can also stick around after the festival on Friday for a memorial concert by The American Symphony Orchestra on the 25th anniversary of 9/11. No tickets are required for the concert.

If you’re celebrating Rosh Hashanah and don’t want to cook, check out these restaurants that are hosting feasts:

  • Mile End Deli

  • Kubeh

  • Hearth

  • Balaboosta for a pick up option

Saturday September 12

Pig Island NYC
Snug Harbor Cultural Center | 12-4pm at 1000 Richmond Terrace, Staten Island

Pig Island is an all-you-can-eat-and-drink outdoor food festival dedicated to barbecue and whole-hog cooking. More than a dozen chefs and pitmasters will be serving everything from whole-hog roasts and pork belly to Caribbean, Puerto Rican, Thai and Carolina-style barbecue, alongside local beer, cider, wine and spirits. There’s also a hot sauce alley, butchering demonstrations and a vegetable grilling station. Tickets start at $60 and include unlimited food and drinks.

⭐ Pop Talks: How Shonda Rhimes Changed Television
Grove 34 Comedy Club | 7-9pm at 31-83 34th St, Astoria

Pop Talks is a lecture series dedicated to breaking down major moments and figures in pop culture, and this edition is all about Shonda Rhimes. Writer and editor Lindsay Denninger will look at how shows like Grey’s Anatomy and Scandal, and characters like Meredith Grey and Olivia Pope, changed television and influenced pop culture more broadly. There will also be themed cocktails, food, and time for conversation after the talk. Tickets are $29.

Ernesto’s Annual Block Party
Ernesto’s | 3-10pm at 259 East Broadway, Lower East Side

Basque restaurant Ernesto’s is taking over the street outside the restaurant for its third annual end-of-summer block party. There’ll be DJs playing throughout the afternoon and evening, including Ali Mae and Roman Chappelle, plus outdoor stations serving Ernesto’s Basque pintxos and oysters and a walk-up bar inside for cocktails. Last year’s party drew more than 1,000 people, so this should be a big one. Free to attend with no RSVP required. Check out full details here.

Sunday September 13

⭐ All In at Union Square Cafe
Union Square Cafe | 3pm at 101 E 19th St, Union Square

Union Square Cafe’s annual restaurant industry fundraiser brings together a pretty great lineup of NYC restaurants for an afternoon of unlimited food and drinks. Tickets include bites from Ambassadors Clubhouse, Borgo, Strange Delight, Daily Provisions, Island Creek Oysters and more, Caffè Panna ice cream, plus an open bar with beer, wine and cocktails from Kabawa. 100% of proceeds go to three nonprofits that provide culinary training, education and career opportunities in hospitality. Tickets are $125.

400 Years on the Bowery
The Municipal Art Society of NYC | 11am-1pm in the Bowery (exact location on RSVP)

The Municipal Art Society leads a two-hour walking tour through 400 years of Bowery history, from its beginnings as a Native American footpath and Dutch farm road to its eras as NYC’s first entertainment district, an infamous skid row, and eventually a center for art and punk. Along the way, guide and author David Mulkins will trace the neighborhood’s connections to vaudeville, Yiddish theater, tap dance, tattooing, Houdini, Abstract Expressionism and CBGB-era punk, while stopping at architectural landmarks including the Bowery Savings Bank and Cooper Union. Tickets are $35.

What I did last week.

I was in Portugal celebrating two wonderful friends tying the knot and took last week off from the letter. I’ve officially capped out my 2 “City Happenings vacation weeks” for the year, which is my totally self imposed policy. So expect to catch the letter every Monday for the rest of 2026.

item.title: Things to Do in NYC This Week (Aug 24 - 30)
item.description: Ugly Baby returns, free jazz, and a Chinatown block party
item.dc:creator: Alexa Weiser
item.content:encoded:
A slightly late-breaking City Happenings this week! I usually get this into your inbox on Monday mornings, but this week got away from me. Luckily, most of the good stuff is still ahead.

Tuesday August 25

⭐ Spritz Soirée
Hudson VU Rooftop | 6-9pm at 653 Eleventh Ave, Hell’s Kitchen

Hudson VU is squeezing in one more very summery rooftop night with a Spritz Soirée dedicated to the Italian tradition of aperitivo. You’ll get unlimited Aperol, Hugo, and Lolea spritzes alongside two hours of passed Italian-inspired bites, cheese, and charcuterie, all with views over the city. Tickets are $78 and include all drinks and food.

Subscribe for the best things to do in NYC.

Word Play Social: SpeakEasy
Beltane | 6:30-9pm at 10 E 16th St, Union Square

A happy hour for people who are obsessed with the English language. Two CUNY linguistics professors will give short talks, one on words that don’t have simple English translations and another on how our brains learn to create words and sentences we’ve never heard before (and how that differs from AI). There’s a Q&A followed by word games and drinks. Tickets start at $5.

Wednesday August 26

From Summer to Autumn: A TCM Wellness Workshop with Kamwo
Think!Chinatown | 6:30-8pm at 1 Pike St, Chinatown

Think!Chinatown and neighborhood institution Kamwo Meridian Herbs are hosting a workshop on how traditional Chinese medicine approaches the transition from summer to fall. The evening includes herbal tea, ear seeding, self-massage, a debloating wintermelon herbal soup, and a lesson from acupuncturist and herbalist Olivia Choi on seasonal wellness and different Chinese herbs. Tickets are sliding scale starting at $15.

⭐ UNMUTED Debate: Bets Over Baghdad, or Our Kalshi Crisis
Unmuted | 6:30-8:30pm in Brooklyn (RSVP for address)

Prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket increasingly let people bet real money on everything from elections to ceasefires. This debate takes on whether that makes them a useful way to aggregate information or whether there are some things we simply shouldn’t be able to profit from predicting. A political science professor and former Citadel trader argue opposite sides, followed by discussion and drinks. Tickets are $30 and include drinks.

WFMU Literary Guild
The Red Room at KGB Bar | 7-9pm at 85 E 4th St, East Village

The DJs behind freeform radio station WFMU apparently have plenty to say when they’re off the air too. Their quarterly Literary Guild brings WFMU DJs and friends together to read whatever they’ve been writing, which can mean short stories, essays and poems but also letters to Prince, micro-memoirs, selected tweets, and other things that don’t really fit a single category. Sounds wonderfully weird. Entry is free with a two-drink minimum.

Thursday August 27

⭐ One Good Work Opening Reception
Prospect Heights Art Club x Studio Contro | 6pm at 623 Bergen St, Prospect Heights

Prospect Heights Art Club is a neighborhood arts organization that creates opportunities for local artists to make and show work. Their latest project, One Good Work, brought artists together for a six-month public art residency focused on pushing themselves to create one ambitious piece through research, experimentation, and lots of iteration. The finished works are going on view at Studio Contro for two weeks, kicking off with an opening reception Thursday with wine and the artists. There will also be talks, readings, and other programming throughout the run. Admission is pay what you can, with a suggested $10 donation.

Ugly Baby Reopens
Williamsburg | Thursday at 364 Grand St, Williamsburg.

While not technically an event, I’m too excited not to feature this one. After closing its beloved Carroll Gardens location in 2024, cult-favorite Thai restaurant Ugly Baby is officially back. Chef Sirichai Sreparplarn is reopening in Williamsburg with a space roughly twice the size of the original. There’s even a new menu that promises to go beyond the fiercely spicy regional Thai dishes that made Ugly Baby famous. Reservations will probably be pretty scarce for the next few weeks.

The Wisdom Bar: Sex, Crime, Gender
Fabrik NYC | 5:30-8:30pm at 12-16 Vestry Street, Tribeca

The Wisdom Bar hosts expert-led lectures in bars and other social spaces, and this one is focused on the history of censorship in Hollywood. The evening starts with a screening of the 1933 film Design for Living, followed by film historian Matt Johnson discussing the surprisingly provocative movies of the Pre-Code era, how religious and political pressure led Hollywood to adopt strict censorship rules, and the ways filmmakers found to work around them. The talk will also connect that history to current debates around censorship. Tickets are $37 and include craft beer and snacks.

Friday August 28

⭐ Charlie Parker Jazz Festival
City Parks Foundation | August 28-30 in Harlem & the East Village

The Charlie Parker Jazz Festival returns for its 34th year with three days of free performances in the neighborhoods where the legendary saxophonist lived and worked. It opens Friday night at Marcus Garvey Park with the Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra, followed by a five-hour Saturday lineup headlined by saxophonist Joshua Redman. On Sunday, the festival moves downtown to Tompkins Square Park for Ravi Coltrane, the Billy Hart Quartet, Kassa Overall, and Vanisha Gould. There are also smaller jazz events happening throughout the week, including garden concerts and an after-party jam. All events are completely free.

The Edge of the Abyss: The Music and Legacy of Sofia Gubaidulina
InfraSound | Friday-Sunday at 239 W 49th St, Times Square

Part concert series, part memorial, and part community gathering, this three-day festival celebrates the work of Sofia Gubaidulina, the influential composer who died last year. Friday kicks off with a free discussion featuring musicians who worked directly with Gubaidulina, followed by a community jam where you can bring your own instrument or voice. Saturday is devoted to her solo and duo works, while Sunday closes with a chamber music concert and post-festival reception. Friday is free and weekend tickets are $30 each.

Saturday August 29

¡Wepa! Summer Salsa Social
Hispanic Society Museum & Library | 3-5pm at 613 W 155th St, Washington Heights

The Hispanic Society is turning Audubon Terrace into a salsa floor for the afternoon. The first half hour is an introductory lesson for anyone who needs it, followed by 90 minutes of open dancing with live music. It’s open to complete beginners and experienced dancers alike. If it rains, they’ll move the whole thing inside to the museum’s Main Court. RSVP for free.

⭐ Brooklyn Brewery Farewell Party
Brooklyn Brewery | 9pm-midnight at 79 N 11th St, Williamsburg

After more than 30 years, Brooklyn Brewery is saying goodbye to its original Williamsburg home before moving into its new space at 1 Wythe Ave. They’re sending off 79 N 11th with one final party featuring live sets from Brooklyn bands Tony & The Kiki and Sharkswimmer. Entry is first come, first served.

Notes in Nature: Summer Symphonies
Oyster Bay | 5:30-7pm at 1395 Planting Fields Rd, Oyster Bay

Ok technically Long Island, but pretty close. An outdoor classical concert on the grounds of Planting Fields, the historic Gold Coast estate in Oyster Bay. Nine musicians from Long Island Chamber Music will perform works by Grieg, Holst, Florence Price, Corelli and Tchaikovsky in a conductorless chamber format. Bring a blanket or lawn chair and settle in on the grounds. Tickets are $45 and include a glass of wine.

Sunday August 30

⭐ Chinatown Block Party
Think!Chinatown x Chinatown Records | 4-8pm on Mosco Street, Chinatown

Think!Chinatown’s summer block party series wraps up with a Chinatown-meets-the-Bronx edition. DJs from Uptown Vinyl Supreme, Rhythm & Hues, and yiuyiu will go back-to-back with an all-vinyl set spanning sounds from Chinatown, the Bronx, and beyond. There’s also a drop-in printmaking workshop with artist Helen Feng, where you can bring a T-shirt, tote, notebook, or other item to stamp with her custom Chinatown linocuts. Free and no RSVP needed.

Booze and Build
Somethin’ Else | 4-6pm at 445 Albee Square West, Downtown Brooklyn

Like a paint-and-sip, but with Lego bricks instead of paint. Your ticket gets you access to a bunch of building sets, from botanicals and cats to pirate ships, plus bins of loose bricks if you’d rather freestyle. There’ll also be building competitions, drinking games, and prizes throughout the afternoon. Tickets are $23.

⭐ Symmetry Stroll in Historic Bed-Stuy
Mo Math | 9:30-11am at Fulton Park, Bed-Stuy

A walking tour for anyone who’s deeply interested in brownstone history. MoMath mathematician Chaim Goodman-Strauss leads a one-mile loop through the Bed-Stuy neighborhood, using its Victorian architecture to teach you how to spot the reflections, rotations and other geometric patterns hidden in façades, friezes and decorative details. Doesn’t get more New York than this. Tickets are $30.

What I did last week.

Places or shows I went to over the last week. These are personal recommendations. If I had a cool week, they’ll be cool. If I didn’t, they won’t.

  1. Initio - I visited Initio’s new boutique and learned that I have a very consistent fragrance type: anything that smells like wood. I know this for a fact because of their “Feel Lab”, where you smell different scents blindfolded while sensors track how your brain responds to each one. It’s free to try with no purchase necessary and a very fun way to discover what you actually gravitate toward.

  2. Chloe Radcliffe: CHEAT - This was SO funny. Chloe Radcliffe’s one-woman show is about her history of cheating in relationships, which is a hard premise to pull off, but she’s so vulnerable about it that it ends up being both hilarious and emotional. It’s been extended with new dates in September, so you can still catch it at Joe’s Pub.

  3. Pangat - A friend had to give up a prime-time reservation at Pangat last minute and I was very happy to take it off his hands. The Mumbai street bites were the highlight for me, and I’m mostly just thrilled to have finally found an Indian restaurant I really love in my neighborhood(ish).

  4. ODRE - I squeezed in one last visit to ODRE during its final few days of service for a three-night pop-up with Oilje, a tiny 12-seat restaurant in Seoul that serves just one dish: miyeokguk, Korean seaweed soup traditionally eaten on birthdays. For the pop-up, they turned that tradition into a six-course tasting menu. Very sadly, ODRE itself closed right after the pop-up, but I had to highlight my wonderful experience anyway.

  5. Summer Stage: Chance - I’ve been seeing Chance the Rapper live since my college days, so this one was mostly nostalgia for me. Always very fun to dance outside, though SummerStage concerts seem to be getting more and more crowded. Next time I’ll plan to arrive much earlier for a good spot or just spend up for bleacher seats.

item.title: Things to Do in NYC This Week (Aug 17 - 24)
item.description: Year-round outdoor dining is back
item.dc:creator: Alexa Weiser
item.content:encoded:
The City Council voted Thursday to once again let restaurants keep roadway dining setups up through the winter, reversing the current rules that require them to come down between the end of November and April. I know these are controversial, but I’m personally thrilled.

I love eating outside. I will choose an outdoor table in temperatures that definitely don’t warrant one and that usually annoy the people I’m with. But I also love anything that makes it a little easier for restaurants to succeed in a city that already makes it incredibly hard to run one. Bring on the heated huts this winter.

Monday August 17

Baby Rose Pop-Up
Vinyl + Thread | 12pm at 55 Anchorage Pl, Dumbo

Singer Baby Rose is taking time out from her 4 nights at MSG to pop up at Vinyl + Thread for a meet-and-greet and signing. No RSVP needed, you can just drop by. If you haven’t been, Vinyl + Thread is also worth wandering around while you’re there. The shop combines rare vinyl, vintage clothing, DJ sets, and occasional live performances. The space was opened by the family behind the former Canal Room.

Subscribe for the best things to do in NYC.

Dangerous Docs 2026: States of Emergency
Rooftop Films | 7pm at 9th Ave & Gansevoort St, Meatpacking

Rooftop Films is taking over Gansevoort Plaza for a free outdoor screening of seven documentary shorts about people living through different forms of catastrophe. The films range from extreme heat in Phoenix to melting glaciers and the aftermath of the LA wildfires. Seating opens at 7pm, films start at 8:15pm, and there’s a filmmaker Q&A afterward. RSVP for free.

Tuesday August 18

⭐ Storytelling Showcase & Festival Closing Party
Think!Chinatown | 6:30-8:30pm at 1 Pike St, Chinatown

Think!Chinatown is wrapping up its annual Chinatown Storytelling Festival with a showcase of new projects from local storytellers selected through the festival’s open call. Each person will present their work followed by a short discussion, before the night turns into a closing reception where you can meet the storytellers and celebrate the end of the festival. RSVP with a donation.

The Late Show Writers Present: A Night of Comedy
The Bell House | 7:30pm at 149 7th St, Gowanus

It’s been three months since The Late Show with Stephen Colbert went off the air, and its former writing staff is reuniting for a variety show to show off what they’ve been working on since. The lineup includes a dozen of the show’s writers and comedians, including New Yorker cartoonist Asher Perlman, Michael Cruz Kayne, Eliana Kwartler, Delmonte Bent, Maya Elany, Gabe Gronli, and more. Important clarification before anyone gets too excited: Stephen Colbert himself will not be there. Tickets are $25.

⭐ All Aboard Yelp NYC
NYC Ferry x Yelp | Starting at 4:50pm around NYC

Yelp NYC is taking over an NYC Ferry for a floating summer party celebrating the release of its new list of the 50 Most Saved NYC Attractions, aka the museums, jazz clubs, vintage stores, and other spots New Yorkers are currently bookmarking most. If NYC Ferry’s unhinged and hilarious Instagram account is any indication, I have high hopes for anything their marketing team is involved in. The ferry will have vintage photo ops, tarot readings, carnival games, a subway violinist, caviar bumps, mocktails, and treats from local businesses. A pretty great way to see the skyline at sunset. The event is free and open to anyone with a Yelp account, but you’ll need to RSVP and purchase a regular ferry ticket.

Wednesday August 19

Chloe Radcliffe: CHEAT
Joe’s Pub | Wednesday & Thursday at 7pm at 425 Lafayette St, Noho

Comedian Chloe Radcliffe has cheated in every relationship she’s ever been in, and she’s turned that history into a 75-minute solo show about why. CHEAT uses stand-up and storytelling to dig into her own pattern of infidelity, what happens when you try to suppress the parts of yourself you’re ashamed of, and what it means to actually admit when you’ve hurt people. Radcliffe, who wrote for The Tonight Show and appears in Bradley Cooper’s Is This Thing On?, performs the solo show at Joe’s Pub Wednesday and Thursday night. Tickets are $30.

Outdoor Cinema: The Wild Robot
Parklife | 8pm at 636 Degraw St, Gowanus

Parklife is bringing back its outdoor movie nights, screening films in its big backyard throughout the summer. This week they’re showing The Wild Robot, the Oscar-nominated animated movie about a robot who gets stranded on an island and slowly befriends its animal inhabitants. The movie starts at 8pm but you can grab dinner and drinks and make a night of it. You can technically walk in but I’d make a reservation if you want a good view of the screen.

Thursday August 20

⭐ Amigas Coffee Talk with Denise Soler Cox
Amigas Means Friends x Saturn Road | 10-11:30am at 276 Court St, Cobble Hill

Amigas Means Friends is a community focused on bringing women together through gatherings and conversations designed to make it easier to form real friendships. This week, they’re hosting an intimate morning conversation with author Denise Soler Cox during the launch week of her new book, What Will They Say?. The discussion will explore the cultural expectations that can push women to make themselves smaller, touching on ambition, self-worth, belonging, and the pressure to be the “good” daughter, partner, or employee. It’s meant to be participatory rather than a traditional author talk, with guided discussions and opportunities to connect with other women throughout. Tickets are $15.

Block Printing Workshop with JOYN
Annie’s Blue Ribbon General Store | 7:30-9:30pm at 232 5th Ave, Park Slope

Annie’s Blue Ribbon General Store is teaming up with JOYN for an evening of block printing led by the brand’s founder, Amy Philip. You’ll get a quick history of the craft before choosing from hand-carved wooden blocks and learning traditional printing techniques to create your own patterned ruffle bag, plus a few prints on cotton paper to take home. Tickets are $85 and include all materials, wine, and light bites. No prior experience is necessary!

Friday August 21

Book Release: Every Leaf, Every Stem
Public Records | 5pm at 233 Butler St, Gowanus

Cook and recipe developer Pierce Abernathy is celebrating the release of his debut cookbook, Every Leaf, Every Stem, with a launch party in The Nursery at Public Records. The book focuses on vegetable-forward cooking and making use of the whole plant, including parts that often get discarded. Tickets are $52 and include a copy of the book, snacks, and a welcome drink.

Mosaic Pottery Workshop
Maayan Adin’s Studio | 6:30pm at 265 W 37th St, Midtown

Spend a candlelit evening making your own mosaic pottery piece using air-dry clay, shells, natural stones, vintage charms, and other little treasures. You’ll learn two beginner-friendly pottery techniques and can turn your creation into anything from a jewelry box or candle holder to a bud vase or decorative plate. All materials are included, plus a glass of wine and varnish to finish your piece at home. Tickets are $85.

Saturday August 22

Black Art Library Conversation & Book Swap
The Drawing Center | 4-6pm at 35 Wooster St, Soho

The Drawing Center is hosting a conversation and book swap alongside its current residency of Detroit’s Black Art Library. Black Art Library founder Asmaa Walton will be joined by OlaRonke Akinmowo of The Free Black Women’s Library and scholar and curator Myron Beasley to discuss the role libraries play in Afro-Diasporic communities as spaces for refuge, restoration, and power. There’s also a book swap, so bring up to three gently loved books on art or culture, art writing, or children’s books and leave with something new. Register for free.

Philosophy at the Museum: Ancient Greek and Roman Art
Philosophy Club | 7-9pm at 1000 Fifth Ave, Upper East Side

Philosophy Club is turning a trip through The Met’s Greek and Roman galleries into a group philosophy discussion. You’ll move through the collection looking at ancient statues, jewelry, and pottery and use the works as jumping-off points to talk about ideas like virtue, honor, community, the gods, and the human body. Rather than a traditional museum tour, the night is broken into three 30-minute conversations in small groups of 3-4, with prompts to guide each discussion. Register for free.

Fixing the American Healthcare System (in 2 Days)
Brooklyn Art Haus | Saturday & Sunday at 24 Marcy Ave, Williamsburg

Comedians Ian Goldstein and Emily Menez are attempting the modest task of fixing the American healthcare system over a two-day comedy festival. The weekend brings together comedians, writers, cartoonists, and storytellers for four different shows, including a variety show, healthcare cartoon comedy, satire and storytelling, and a closing game show celebrating the system they have presumably fixed by then. Tickets are free (unlike your healthcare).

Sunday August 23

⭐ Garden Party at Plus de Vin
Children’s Atlas of Wine x Plus de Vin | 6-8pm at 445 Graham Ave, Williamsburg

James Sligh of Children’s Atlas of Wine is taking over the backyard at Plus de Vin for an end-of-summer garden party combining wine, art, and a little arts and crafts. You’ll taste five wines from the latest Children’s Atlas wine club shipment, color in maps, browse an art print showcase, and get a copy of ITALY, a new zine about NYC wine programs and their relationship to the Italian natural wine scene. I’ve been to a few of James’s events and love that he makes learning about wine feel a little like being a kid again: drawing maps, making things, and getting curious about why places and grapes are the way they are. Tickets are $40.

Poetry in Elizabeth Street Garden
Elizabeth Street Garden x McNally Jackson | 5-7pm at 211 Elizabeth St, Nolita

Elizabeth Street Garden feels like an actual neighborhood backyard, with free live music, tai chi, workshops, and a bi-weekly poetry series with McNally Jackson. This Sunday’s theme is “Blue,” and anyone can submit a poem in advance for a chance to read it in the garden. Even if you’re not getting behind the mic, it’s a fun way to spend a summer evening. Free and open to the public. Check out their full calendar of events.

⭐ Full Crate Kitchen 007: Wish You Were Here
Full Crate Kitchen x StoryTell | 6:30-10pm at 299 S 4th St, Williamsburg

Full Crate Kitchen turns albums into dinner parties, creating multi-course menus designed around the music and story of a single record. For their seventh edition, they’re taking on Pink Floyd’s Wish You Were Here, with a seven-course menu inspired by the album’s themes of absence, disillusionment, and the pressure of following up The Dark Side of the Moon. You’ll eat as the album plays on vinyl, with guided storytelling and conversation woven throughout the night. Tickets are $155 and include dinner and two drinks. The menu stays secret until you’re there.

Yoga and Cake
Kala Yoga | 1:30pm at 783 Driggs Ave, Williamsburg

Exactly as it sounds: one hour of yoga followed by one slice of homemade cake. The all-levels vinyasa class includes a playful flow, music, and restorative rest before everyone hangs out over cake, with this week’s flavors inspired by sweet corn, blueberry, and mascarpone. Mats and props are provided, so you really just have to show up and earn your cake. Tickets are $26.

What I did last week.

Places or shows I went to over the last week. These are personal recommendations. If I had a cool week, they’ll be cool. If I didn’t, they won’t.

  1. Grimm Tavern - The new project by Grimm Ales finally opened on Vanderbilt in the old Olmsted space. They inherited arguably the best backyard in the neighborhood and the burger is pretty good too. I also love that they’re open for lunch during the week. I can see this becoming a good cafe alternative when I want to work somewhere that serves fries.

  2. Flower Cat Cafe - Really cute and whimsical cafe in Greenpoint. Almost felt Wonderland themed. They have sidewalk seating and sell flower bouquets too. While I didn’t go for an event I saw that they also host readings and other happenings on their calendar.

  3. Bolo Bolo - I guess this was a week of cute cafes. This one I’d recommend more as a pit stop while wandering stores in Cobble Hill since it’s pretty tiny. The specialty lattes are the main draw. I’m usually a black drip girl myself, but I had to try the pistachio cream latte and I was not disappointed.

  4. Print Center New York - I had never been to Print Center New York before. It’s a free nonprofit space dedicated entirely to printed art. Their current exhibition, New Voices: Design, features eight emerging artists using printmaking to explore pattern, from woodcuts and textiles to more experimental works. It's a small and easy to pop into to see something new. I’ll be keeping an eye on their upcoming exhibition and workshop calendar.

item.title: Things to Do in NYC This Week (Aug 10 - 16)
item.description: Cheese parties, vintage trains & summer jazz
item.dc:creator: Alexa Weiser
item.content:encoded:
I spent this weekend in the Catskills with a group of friends from my first job out of college, celebrating what we realized was our 10 year reunion since our intern summer. It feels way too soon to be saying that, but the math is the math.

I've naturally made fewer close friends through work as I've gotten older. I think that's partly just what happens when you already have an established life outside of it. But your first job is different. At least mine was. We were all figuring out how to work and how to be adults in New York. And there wasn't much separation between the two. The people I worked with became the people I went out with, spent weekends with and, in my case, eventually met my husband through.

The funniest evidence of how much that one workplace shaped all of our lives is that of the six couples in the Catskills this weekend, four met through that first job. Which is an absolutely insane hit rate. I don't think I'd ever want my work and social life to be that intertwined again, but I'm very glad it was at 21.

Monday August 10

⭐ 45th Annual Battery Dance Festival
Robert F. Wagner Jr. Park | August 10-16 at 20 Battery Pl, Battery Park City

New York’s longest running free public dance festival returns for its 45th year with a full week of performances from dance companies and artists from New York and around the world. The festival kicks off Monday with four free outdoor community dance workshops starting at 4pm, before the professional performances begin Tuesday night. From there, a different lineup takes the stage outdoors at 7pm each evening through Sunday, spanning contemporary dance, flamenco, traditional Ecuadorian and Indian dance, and companies visiting from Spain, Brazil, Taiwan and Romania. All performances are free. Check out the full schedule.

Subscribe for the best things to do in NYC.

Burning Bridges Summer BBQ
Bridges x Barbichette | 5-9:30pm at 9 Chatham Sq, Chinatown

Bridges is throwing its first proper summer BBQ with Barbichette, a natural wine producer making wine exclusively from New York grown fruit. The standing party will have stations set up throughout the restaurant pouring Barbichette wines alongside grilled bites and summer snacks from the Bridges team. Upon entry you get a bingo card covering five dishes and two drinks from stations around the room. Tickets are $110.

Tuesday August 11

⭐ Chinatown Storytelling Festival: Through the Years
Think!Chinatown x DCTV Firehouse Cinema | 7-8:30pm at 87 Lafayette St, Chinatown

Think!Chinatown is approaching its 10th anniversary, and they’re digging into a decade of archives for a 90-minute retrospective of the neighborhood stories they’ve documented along the way. The program brings together animated shorts, oral histories, dance and documentary films about Chinatown’s people and history, from memories of its once-booming garment factories and immigrant life to local activists, musicians and artists. It also includes a new animated short about the humble feather duster, part of a series that uses everyday Chinatown objects to tell larger community stories. The screening is part of both Think!Chinatown’s Chinatown Storytelling Festival and the Asian American International Film Festival. Tickets are $16.

Mahjong Lessons & Supervised Play
Chaotic Good Cafe | 7-9pm at 200 W 84th St, Upper West Side

If you’ve been wanting to learn mahjong but don’t know where to start, board game cafe Chaotic Good Cafe is hosting an evening specifically for beginners. Resident mahjong teacher Sawyer will walk everyone through the basics in a group lesson before sticking around for supervised play, so you can actually practice with someone there to answer questions and correct you as you go. It’s limited to 8 people so that you get hands on attention. Tickets are $60.

Wednesday August 12

Salsa by the Water
Domino Park | 6-9pm at 15 River St, Williamsburg

Salsa by the Water is back for its sixth season at Domino Square, with free salsa lessons followed by live music and dancing along the waterfront every other Wednesday. Opening night features Uptown Royalty, with lessons from Nieves Latin Dance Studio starting at 6:15pm before the band takes over at 7:15pm. Dancing with strangers with the Manhattan skyline as your backdrop is really special. RSVP for free.

Girl Dinner Paint & Sip
Pour Toi | 6:30-9pm at 157 Ludlow St, Lower East Side

Pour Toi’s monthly blind box paint and sip gives everyone an art kit, but keeps what you’re actually painting a mystery until the night begins. This month’s theme is Girl Dinner, inspired by the chaotic assortment of foods that constitute a meal. The night will start with you mingling and grabbing drinks and bites before your prompt is revealed and you get your curated moodboard for inspiration. Tickets are $38.

Thursday August 13

⭐ Emmys Round Table & Q&A
W New York | 6-8pm at 1567 Broadway, Times Square

Ahead of the Emmys, W New York is bringing together five of the people behind some of this year’s biggest shows for a conversation about the craft of television. Editors from Hacks, Beef, and SNL will join the costume designer behind Sirens and VFX supervisor from The Penguin to share behind the scenes stories and answer audience questions. The panel discussion will be followed by a reception and cocktail. RSVP for free.

Fashion in Frame: Yves Saint Laurent
ICP | 6:30-8pm at 84 Ludlow St, Lower East Side

ICP is pairing its current Yves Saint Laurent and Photography exhibition with a conversation about how photography helped shape the designer’s career and public image. Fashion historian Raissa Bretaña and ICP Creative Director David Campany will trace Saint Laurent from his first haute couture collection in 1962 through his work in film, including Belle du Jour, and his growing presence in front of the camera. The $5 ticket also includes gallery admission, so you can see the exhibition before the talk.

Poetry & Pours: A Wine and Poetry Tasting
June Wine Bar | 7-9pm at 231 Court St, Cobble Hill

Local poets Sharon Lin and Stephanie Niu have selected poems to pair with five seasonal wines from June Wine Bar, matching each reading to the sensory qualities, mood and tasting notes of the glass. Over two hours, they’ll guide the group through the wine flight with live poetry readings along the way, exploring how taste can change the way you experience a poem and vice versa. I don’t really get how a wine can match a poem but I am intrigued. Tickets are $84.

Friday August 14

Jazzmobile Centennial Tribute Concert
Jazzmobile | 7-9pm at Marcus Garvey Park, Harlem

Jazzmobile has been bringing free jazz into Harlem parks and streets since 1964, and this summer concert celebrates what would have been the 100th birthdays of two NEA Jazz Masters, pianist Randy Weston and saxophonist Jimmy Heath. The ARAQ will perform Weston’s music with a five piece lineup led by saxophonist and flutist T.K. Blue, followed by the Jimmy Heath Big Band under the direction of saxophonist Antonio Hart. No RSVP needed. Check out their full schedule of free shows throughout the summer.

haus Dinner Club
haus | 8pm at a secret location in Manhattan

Longtime friends and chefs Rafael and Riku run haus as a tiny dinner club centered around the kind of food you’d expect from a fine dining restaurant, served more like a dinner party. They build seasonal tasting menus around ingredients sourced from local farmers markets and keep the guest list small, usually around 10 people. Friday’s dinner includes a three course tasting menu and opening cocktail, with an optional premium wine pairing. Tickets are $70 for dinner, plus $40 for the pairing. I think it’s hosted at one of their homes but I’m not entirely sure.

Saturday August 15

⭐ Cheese Party
Metro Cheese Club | 6-10pm at 5-84 Woodward Ave, Ridgewood

There’s nothing bad about a party dedicated to cheese. A group of NYC cheesemongers is throwing an entire party around 150 pounds of all you can eat cheese. Beyond working your way through the spread, there will be cheesemonger improv and stand up, live music, a disco DJ, flash tattoos, caricature drawings, Mario Kart, poetry, games, and a donation based bar. World's Best Cheese is supplying the cheese and accoutrements, and they're asking everyone to bring their own plate, cup, and utensils to cut down on waste. The dress code is "Brooklyn cheese party" which I will leave open to interpretation. Tickets are $25.

Harlem Rides the Range Screening & Conversation
Poster House | 6:30-9pm at 119 W 23rd St, Chelsea

Poster House is screening the 1939 Western Harlem Rides the Range, starring Herbert Jeffries as the “Bronze Buckaroo” and featuring an all Black cast at a time when the genre largely excluded Black performers. The screening ties into the museum’s current Act Black: Posters from Black American Stage & Screen exhibition and will be followed by a conversation on the history of Black Westerns, how these films challenged representations of Black life on screen, and their place in American film history. There will also be an audience Q&A and book signing. RSVP for free.

⭐ Threes Flea
Threes Brewing x Fig Shop | 12-7pm at 113 Franklin St, Greenpoint

Threes Brewing is turning its Greenpoint location into a flea market for the first time, with the day curated by Fig Shop, a vintage project focused on thoughtfully sourced secondhand clothing and more communal ways to shop. They’re bringing together local vendors selling vintage, art, books, and records, with a DJ playing in the afternoon. Grand Army will be handling the food and Threes will have the beer covered, so you can browse and then stick around for a drink. RSVP for free.

The Lupine Series Presents: The Music of James Taylor
El Sol Brillante | 5:30-6:30pm at 522 E 12th St, East Village

The Lupine Series is bringing a seven piece band of local musicians into El Sol Brillante community garden for an hour of James Taylor. The tiny East Village garden has been around since the 1970s and makes an especially nice setting for a neighborhood concert, with the musicians playing among the garden plots rather than on a traditional stage. Free with no RSVP needed.

Sunday August 16

Tie Dye Pop Up
Tacocina | 1pm at 25 S River St, Williamsburg

Taco stand Tacocina is teaming up with a Brooklyn tie dye artist for an afternoon of DIY tie dye in Domino Park. Your ticket gets you a Tacocina t-shirt to dye plus two tacos, and you can bring along any other shirts, bandanas, pillowcases, or whatever else you want to give the tie dye treatment. Margaritas will be available while everything dries in the sun. Tickets are $28.

To the Rockaways by Rail
NY Transit Museum | 10am-5pm departing from 96 St and 2 Av, Upper East Side

The Transit Museum is bringing out three generations of vintage subway cars for a summer ride all the way to the Rockaways. You’ll board a train made up of R10, R16, and R32 “Brightliner” cars at 96th Street and ride to Rockaway Park at Beach 116th Street. Once there, spend a few hours at the beach, walk the boardwalk, or pack a picnic before hopping back aboard the vintage train for the return trip to Manhattan at 3pm. Tickets are $60.

Meditation & Philosophy: Vīrya
New York Philosophy Club | 4-7pm at 151 W 30th St, Midtown

The New York Philosophy Club hosts weekly gatherings built around discussing and questioning philosophical ideas, and this edition adds a meditation component in collaboration with Vīrya. The afternoon starts with an introduction to the nature of awareness and the difference between mindfulness and mindstillness, followed by a 30 minute sound based meditation designed to let the mind settle without actively trying to concentrate. Afterwards, the group moves into a broader philosophical discussion about the ideas raised by the practice. No meditation experience is required, and the conversation is approached from a secular perspective. Tickets are $25.

What I did last week.

Places or shows I went to over the last week. These are personal recommendations. If I had a cool week, they’ll be cool. If I didn’t, they won’t.

  1. WNYC - The highlight of my week was being a guest on WNYC’s All Of It with Alison Stewart. It was my first time doing live radio, or really any sort of audio format, which definitely took me out of my comfort zone but was also really fun. We talked about some of my favorite things to do in Manhattan this summer and even fielded recommendations from callers. If you missed it, you can still listen here.

  2. Shifters - On a limited run at the iconic Cherry Lane Theatre, Shifters jumps back and forth in time to tell the story of two people reconnecting after years apart. The plot itself is relatively simple, but the chemistry between the two leads is electric and completely carries it. See it before it closes August 30.

  3. Cobble Hill Cinemas - I rarely see movies in theaters over the summer, but this heat (and my Tom Holland obsession) has had me seeking out a cool, dark movie theater more often. Cobble Hill Cinemas has none of the frills of the newer theaters but it does have plenty of old-school charm. It’s also often the one place I can find last-minute tickets to a big movie without sitting in the front row. A good one to keep in your back pocket over Alamo Drafthouse or Nitehawk if you live in South Brooklyn.

  4. Poppy - Not only is the sidewalk seating some of the most fun people watching in the city, but every Wednesday you can pop in for free live jazz. A really good date night.

item.title: Things to Do in NYC This Week (Aug 3 - 9)
item.description: My radio debut
item.dc:creator: Alexa Weiser
item.content:encoded:
I have a fun announcement this week.

For the past few years, City Happenings has mostly lived in one format: a weekly email. This Tuesday I’m trying something new.

I’ll be joining WNYC’s All of It with Alison Stewart for her “Summer in the City” series to talk about overlooked things to do in Manhattan. We’ll be chatting about everything from community gardens and dance nights to cultural institutions, neighborhood festivals, and some of my favorite places to escape the heat. There will also be live listener call-ins, which (I’m hoping) means I’ll end up with a few recommendations of my own.

One of the things I love most about writing City Happenings is that it's kept me endlessly curious about New York City. Getting to bring that curiosity to a different format, and hopefully introduce a whole new audience to some of the city's lesser-known corners feels pretty special.

You can tune in live at 12:40pm here.

Monday August 3

⭐ Behind the Menu Premiere Party
Romeo’s | 7pm at 118 St Marks Pl, East Village

Romeo’s is turning its new seven minute mockumentary into a full blown movie premiere. Walk the red carpet, grab popcorn, sparkling wine, tequila cocktails, and dino nuggets, then settle in for the debut of Behind the Menu, a short film about the bar’s delightfully retro VHS menu. It’s exactly the kind of absurd, self aware industry night I’d expect from Romeo’s. No RSVP needed.

Subscribe for the best things to do in NYC.

Film Screening: TCB
Harlem Week | 6-9:30pm at 601 W 125th St, Harlem

Harlem Week is one of New York’s longest running summer festivals, transforming what began as a single block party in 1974 into a month of free events celebrating Harlem’s culture, history, and community. As part of this year’s programming, ImageNation is screening TCB, a documentary on writer, filmmaker, and activist Toni Cade Bambara, followed by a conversation with co-director Louis Massiah and Firelight Media CEO Loira Limbal. RSVP for free.

Tuesday August 4

Quarterly Book Club: Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion
Week Nights | 5:30-7:30pm at 10 E 16th St, Flatiron

Books, Business & Big Ideas is a quarterly book club for people who enjoy unpacking influential nonfiction with a room full of curious strangers. This month's pick is Robert Cialdini's Influence, the classic on the psychology of persuasion that has shaped how marketers, negotiators, and business leaders think about human behavior. There will be a thoughtful discussion on the subtle ways influence shows up in everyday life, from advertising to restaurant menus and everything in between. RSVP for free.

Bingo Night
Farm.One | 7pm at 625 Bergen St, Prospect Heights

Every neighborhood needs their version of Farm.One. The indoor vertical farm and brewery is a masterclass in community building, constantly hosting approachable events that make it easy to meet people and try something new. This week they're hosting bingo night with local host Mickey Nolan, with prizes up for grabs throughout the evening. Free with no RSVP needed.

Wednesday August 5

⭐ In the Mood for Trivia
Sugar Mouse | 8:30pm at 47 3rd Ave, East Village

The 49th Asian American International Film Festival, the country’s longest-running showcase of Asian and Asian American independent cinema, is back this week with screenings, conversations, and special events across the city. One of the more playful additions is this MUBI-sponsored film trivia night, where teams will compete through movie soundtracks, posters, iconic quotes, and other cinematic deep cuts. Tickets are pay-what-you-can, making it an easy way to experience the festival even if you don’t have time to catch a full slate of films.

Dominican Film Festival Opening Night: La Fábrica de Bodas
United Palace | 8:30pm at 4140 Broadway, Washington Heights

The Dominican Film Festival in New York celebrates its 15th year with the world premiere of La Fábrica de Bodas, a comedy about an undocumented Mexican immigrant who enters a marriage arrangement in hopes of securing legal status. The opening night also brings the film’s director and cast to the historic United Palace and marks the start of a festival dedicated to showcasing both emerging and established Dominican filmmakers. If you’ve never been to the United Palace, it’s a great chance to finally see one of the city’s most beautiful theaters. Tickets start at $35.

Thursday August 6

⭐ Care in Creative Industries: Fashion & Design Respond to AIDS
Poster House | 6:30-7:30pm at 119 W 23rd St, Chelsea

Poster House’s excellent Love & Fury: New York’s Fight Against AIDS exhibition continues with a conversation exploring how New York’s fashion and design communities mobilized during the AIDS crisis. Curators, historians, and leaders from the CFDA will discuss the fundraising campaigns, activism, and iconic posters that helped bring grassroots efforts into the mainstream. Tickets are $10.

From Farm to Whisk
Matchaful Ritual Bar | 4pm at 92 Berry St, Williamsburg

I still can’t get behind matcha but my trusted friend said this was cool. This guided tasting breaks down why ceremonial matcha tastes so different from the powder sitting on grocery store shelves. You’ll taste kukicha, tencha, and finished matcha while learning how cultivation, harvesting, and stone milling shape the final cup, leaving with a deeper appreciation for the generations of Japanese tea producers behind it. Tickets are $50 and include a 10g sample of Matchaful’s Tsuyuhikari Limited Reserve.

Dreams of Yesterday Beer Launch Party
Threes Brewing | 5-8pm at 333 Douglass St, Gowanus

Threes Brewing is bringing back Dreams of Yesterday, its pilsner brewed with oyster shells in collaboration with Billion Oyster Project. To celebrate, they’re throwing a launch party with $7 cans, freshly shucked oysters from Grand Army, dirty martini specials, and a DJ spinning all evening. Even better, a portion of every beer sold supports Billion Oyster Project’s work restoring oysters to New York Harbor. RSVP for free.

Friday August 7

New York City Opera: Celebration of Ella Fitzgerald
Bryant Park Picnic Performances | 7pm on the Bryant Park Lawn, Midtown

Pack a picnic blanket and settle in for a free evening celebrating the music of Ella Fitzgerald. As part of Bryant Park’s Picnic Performances series, New York City Opera will present a tribute led by three time Grammy Award winning soprano Latonia Moore, joined by a live band and special guests performing jazz standards and American classics. Free with no RSVP required.

AAIFF Shorts: After Dark
Asian American International Film Festival | 8:30pm at 181-189 2nd Ave, East Village

One of my favorite ways to experience a film festival is through the shorts programs because you get to squeeze in so much. This late night lineup from the Asian American International Film Festival features everything from a mysteriously pregnant goat to a lonely boy who befriends a severed head, alongside stories of ghosts, surreal bus rides, and complicated relationships. Stick around afterward for a Q&A with several of the filmmakers. Tickets are $18.

Neal Francis at Rockaway Music Live
Rockaway Music Live | 7pm at 108-10 Rockaway Beach Dr, Rockaway Beach

Chicago soul and rock musician Neal Francis is playing an outdoor set at The Rockaway Hotel as part of the Rockaway Music Live summer concert series. An outdoor concert a block from the beach is a pretty great way to spend an August evening. Tickets are $41.

Saturday August 8

⭐ Maum Market
Maum | 11am-4pm at Pier 17, Seaport

The original and largest marketplace dedicated to Asian-owned brands returns to Pier 17 this weekend. There will be independent makers, designers, and food businesses alongside brands you’ve probably already seen popping up all over your Instagram. It’s a mix of design-forward home goods, art, fashion, and beauty. My friend got the cutest little onigiri earrings there last year. Register for free.

Dilly Dally Fair
Dilly Dally | Saturday & Sunday from 11am-6pm at 15 E 40th St, Midtown

Part maker’s market, part creative playground, Dilly Dally Fair is built around the idea that you don’t just have to admire handmade work, you can try making it too. Browse more than 40 artists and designers selling ceramics, furniture, textiles, illustrations, jewelry, and other crafted goods, then sign up for one of six hands on workshops ranging from watercolor and incense making to needle felting, kokedama, and even a kintsugi repair ritual. You can really make this a full weekend affair. The fair is free to attend or you can register for workshops starting at $65.

Yappy Hour
Badass Animal Rescue x Penny | 12-4pm at 288 N 8th St, Williamsburg

There are a lot of dog adoption events in the city, but this one got me. Badass Animal Rescue is bringing adoptable dogs to The Penny Hotel’s courtyard for the afternoon, while the rooftop hosts a yappy hour where $1 from every signature cocktail sold is donated back to the rescue. It feels fitting that this is happening at The Penny, a Williamsburg hotel actually named after a dog. Even if you’re not looking to adopt, it’s a way to spend an afternoon surrounded by cute dogs while supporting a good cause. No RSVP needed, check out event details here.

BRIC Celebrates Aaliyah: One in a Million
BRIC | 4pm at the Lena Horne Bandshell, Prospect Park

This year’s BRIC Celebrate Brooklyn! tribute honors Brooklyn-born R&B icon Aaliyah with an afternoon of live performances, DJs, dancers, and stories celebrating her legacy. Music director Taja Cheek of L’Rain leads a lineup featuring Res, serpentwithfeet, Halima, and more, all performing Aaliyah’s biggest hits. RSVP for free.

⭐ Fake Tech Ad Art Show
Fake Tech Ads | 10am-7pm at the W 4th St Subway Station, West Village

I’ve always wondered who the geniuses behind those fake tech startup ads plastered around the subway were. I think they’re absolutely hilarious. Maybe because I work in tech. This Saturday they’re taking over an old newsstand at West 4th with an installation featuring their viral fake ads, plus a chance to make your own, free merch, and, naturally, drinkable Kool-Aid. RSVP for free.

Sunday August 9

Soul Summit Music Festival
Soul Summit | 3-8pm at Fort Greene Park, Fort Greene

For more than two decades, Soul Summit has been turning Fort Greene Park into one of New York’s best outdoor dance floors. The festival showcases artists of various backgrounds, including DJs, bands, dance companies, fashion designers, filmmakers and photographers. Hundreds of people spread out with picnic blankets, food, and friends before making their way to the dance circle. Fort Greene Park on a Sunday is always a good idea but this weekend will be particularly fun. See event details for more info.

An Italian Summer: Drink & Draw
Sunday Gelato x Annie’s Blue Ribbon | 2-4pm at 232 5th Ave, Park Slope

Sunday Gelato is hosting an Italian inspired drawing session in the backyard of Annie's Blue Ribbon General Store. You'll sketch still lifes inspired by Italian food while snacking from a grazing table, then head home with a custom decorated tote bag and a bottle of Graza olive oil, both included with your ticket.

⭐ A Summer Bakery
For Example | 11am-2pm at 402 Graham Ave, Williamsburg

The creative studio, For Example, known for crafting playful food experiences and beautifully designed spaces, is popping up at Land to Sea with a one day summer bakery featuring seasonal pastries and treats inspired by their favorite flavors of the season. RSVP for free.

What I did last week.

Places or shows I went to over the last week. These are personal recommendations. If I had a cool week, they’ll be cool. If I didn’t, they won’t.

  1. OASES - I stopped by OASES to try their new Flamingo Estate collaboration smoothie. The smoothie was great, but I was even happier to discover the space itself. It's bright, beautiful, and spacious. It's also right by my office, so I have a feeling it'll become one of my go-to spots for working between meetings.

  2. Bus Stop Cafe - I grabbed a quick bite with a friend at one of their sidewalk tables and found myself wondering about the history of the space. Turns out it's been serving the neighborhood since the 1960s, first as Bus Stop Coffee Shop before becoming Bus Stop Cafe in 1995. It’s a mix between a diner and a restaurant and still has a classic neighborhood feel that's getting harder to find.

  3. Seiren - Ducked in to escape the rain and ended up having a full dinner of tapas at the bar. It was a very fish-forward menu which is perfect for me. Some of the friendliest staff I’ve encountered in a while too.

  4. Vanity Vintage - Tiny underground vintage store I must walk by 3 times a week. Finally peaked in and I’m glad I did. While I didn’t leave with anything this time, there were some fun finds and I’ll definitely be back.
